title: A conserved astrocyte-like parental cell defines the phylogenetic root of adult-type diffuse glioma

programme.programmeTitle: A conserved astrocyte-like parental cell defines the phylogenetic root of adult-type diffuse glioma

bodyParagraphs: Adult-type diffuse gliomas are among the most lethal human cancers, yet how genetic clonal evolution gives rise to transcriptional heterogeneity has remained unresolved. We assembled one of the largest single-cell atlases of glioma to date, integrating scRNA-seq, snRNA-seq, and spatial transcriptomics across 69 tumours and over 1.2 million cells spanning IDH-mutant astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Coupling transcriptomes to single-cell DNA and mitochondrial lineage markers, we reconstructed phylogenetic clonal evolution and, by defining the parental clonal population, identified a quiescent, astrocyte-like parental cell (ALPC) at the phylogenetic root of every tumour. Orthogonal DNA-and protein-level assays, in situ spatial localisation, and patient-derived stem-permissive cultures validated the ALPC as a conserved, stem-like, differentiation-competent founder compartment. From this apex we resolved seven recurrent transcriptional states—including neural-and oligodendroglial-lineage and proliferative programs—that recapitulate normal neural stem-cell differentiation trajectories. Despite arising from distinct foundational driver alterations, all glioma types converged on a shared hierarchical architecture in which the quiescent parental compartment gives rise to proliferative and lineage-committed progeny. The IDH axis modulated this common framework rather than redefining it: IDH-mutant tumours were dominated by differentiated lineage-like states with relative immune paucity, whereas glioblastoma showed expansion of ALPC and hypoxia states with increased immune infiltration and mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation programs. Together, these findings link clonal evolution to cellular heterogeneity through a conserved developmental framework, repositioning the astrocyte-like parental cell as the lineage-defined root of glioma cell states. Because this founder compartment is shared across subtypes yet sits upstream of all malignant progeny, eliminating it may offer pan-glioma therapeutic opportunities.

title: A transgenic glioblastoma mouse model containing a reporter element for stem-like tumor cells.

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) cells endowed with stem-like properties (GSCs) can have increased potential for tumor (relapse) formation and often display accelerated resistance to standard therapy. Hence, obtaining strategies for therapeutic targeting of GSCs is a priority in neurooncology. To address this issue, we developed a transgenic mouse model faithfully recapitulating human disease and also containing a reporter function for GSCs. Histopathologically, the experimental tumors contain all hallmarks of human GBM. Tumors are induced after subventricular injection of a hybrid AAV (providing flexibility for the time-point of tumor initiation) and the vector assures target-specific recombination (in neural precursor cells). The vector contains sufficient payload in order to accommodate different proto-oncogenes or can drive the expression of imaging markers like luciferase in order to monitor tumor growth in real-time. Furthermore, cre-recombinase induced expression of RFP allows tracing of tumor cells on the clonal level. Cross-breading the model with another transgenic mouse strain harboring a modified nestin-promoter element driving GFP expression resulted in combined RFP/GFP expression in a subpopulation of GBM cells. Purification of RFP+/GFP+ cells and orthotopic re-implantation of sorted cells in three consecutive experimental cycles revealed that 500 RFP+/GFP+ are sufficient to generate GBM whereas inoculation of 50,000 RFP+/GFP-negative GBM cells was insufficient to induce tumorigenesis. In addition to their self-renewal capacity throughout in vivo experimentation, the RFP+/GFP+ also showed accelerated self-renewal in vitro (in a limiting dilution assay). Cultivation of RFP+/GFP+ cells over several passages and recapitulation of the serial implantation experiment indicated that RFP+/GFP+ retain their stem-like capacity throughout in vitro maintenance. Overall, we describe an experimental model with profound potential for translational research on GBM.

bodyParagraphs: Successful metastatic colonization requires cancer cells to survive the multiple stresses encountered during early organ adaptation, yet how metastasis-initiating cells overcome this bottleneck remains poorly understood. Here we identify a transient MXD4-dependent proliferative pause that enables aggressive cancer cells to survive early stages of brain colonization. Prior to vascular co-option-associated outgrowth, metastatic cells temporarily restrain proliferation through the MYC antagonist MXD4, allowing them to buffer diverse stress sources encountered after extravasation. Genetic disruption of MXD4 compromises micrometastatic survival and prevents progression to macrometastases. Analyses of human brain micrometastases obtained from autopsies validate the presence of this transient adaptive state in patient samples. Exploiting vulnerabilities associated with the proliferative pause revealed preventive therapeutic opportunities across multiple experimental settings, including spontaneous brain metastasis models and minimal residual disease following neurosurgical resection. In addition, patient-derived organotypic cultures containing invasive fronts confirmed the feasibility of targeting this state using clinically available drugs. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized adaptive stage during metastatic colonization and identify actionable vulnerabilities that could be exploited to prevent brain metastasis progression and relapse.

bodyParagraphs: Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas exhibit variable treatment response and patient outcomes. To

better understand the genetic and cellular changes that drive IDH-mutant glioma progression, we analyzed longitudinally collected whole-genome/whole-exome datasets from 183 IDH-mutant glioma patients available through the Glioma Longitudinal AnalySiS (GLASS) Consortium, combined with single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling of 75 temporally separated tumors across 35 oligodendroglioma/astrocytoma patients. At recurrence, we observed enrichment of hypermutation across glioma types, astrocytoma-specific CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion and focal oncogene amplifications, and oligodendroglioma-specific PI3K/NOTCH point mutations. Astrocytomas but not oligodendrogliomas often additionally acquired new chromosomal imbalances, which converged with chromosomal instability markers such as chromothripsis, whole-genome doubling and radiation-treatment associated ID8. Non-hypermutated temolozomide-treated oligodendrogliomas showed a significant enrichment in SBS119, indicating a distinct mechanism for resolving temozolomide-induced damage. These findings show that the genomes of oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas adapt to the selective pressures of tumor progression and treatment in distinct manners. We next asked whether glioma progression may be associated with changes in cell states. We found that malignant cell states across both tumor types transcriptionally resemble stages of normal glial-neuronal lineage development or a reactive mesenchymal-like state. Longitudinal analysis highlighted similar malignant cell state transition patterns in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas. Specifically, tumors that acquired recurrence-associated genetic events, including treatment-associated hypermutation, increased copy number alterations, and cell cycle alterations, showed reduced lineage differentiation and increased proliferative malignant cells at recurrence. An increase in mesenchymal-like state abundance occurred independently of acquired genetic alterations, while no other cell state changes were observed in tumors with relatively stable genomes. Thus, despite clear differences in how astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma genomes adapt to treatment-induced selective pressures, both tumor types converge on shared transcriptionally-defined malignant cell states that associate with reduced overall survival. Our results show that oligodendrogliomas and astrocytomas diverge in genetic response to treatment but converge on cell state adaptations.

title: Adding a Metabolic Layer to Glioblastoma Pathology with Label-Free NADH-Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging

bodyParagraphs: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by profound spatial heterogeneity that cannot be fully captured by conventional histopathology. While hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining and immunohistochemistry define tissue architecture and molecular markers, they fail to reveal the metabolic states underlying tumor progression and therapeutic response. We investigated whether label-free NADH Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (NADH-FLIM) could provide an additional functional layer of information by mapping metabolic heterogeneity directly in clinical specimens. Methods: NADH-FLIM was applied to archived formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) GBM sections. Phasor analysis of endogenous NADH autofluorescence was used to quantify the free/bound NADH fraction (fB-NADH), enabling spatial characterization of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and glycolytic metabolism across distinct histopathological regions. Metabolic profiles were further correlated with genetic drivers by immunohistochemistry. Results: NADH-FLIM identified distinct, statistically significant metabolic signatures associated with major GBM hallmarks. Regions of microvascular proliferation showed significantly higher fB-NADH than adjacent normal-appearing tissue (p<0.0001), consistent with an OXPHOS-dominant phenotype. Pseudopalisading cells surrounding necrosis displayed a significantly lower fB-NADH than the tumor core (p<0.001), indicating a glycolytic shift associated with hypoxic adaptation. Isolated infiltrating tumor cells in perineural and perivascular satellitosis, as well as within histologically normal-appearing brain parenchyma, showed a shift toward a more glycolytic fB-NADH profile compared with the tumor core (p<0.001). FGFR3-positive tumor cells showed a shift toward OXPHOS metabolism compared with adjacent FGFR3-negative cells. Conclusions: NADH-FLIM complements conventional pathology by providing a quantitative, label-free functional map of GBM metabolism while preserving tissue architecture. This approach uncovers metabolically distinct niches that are invisible to routine histology and links oncogenic alterations, including FGFR3::TACC3 fusion, to bioenergetic states. These findings support NADH-FLIM as a promising platform for precision neuropathology and future AI-assisted diagnostic and predictive workflows.

title: Antitumor Activity of All-Trans Retinoic Acid and Curcumin-Loaded BSA Nanoparticles Against U87 Glioblastoma Cells

bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, characterized by intrinsic drug resistance, invasive growth, and the presence of the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which together render standard therapies largely ineffective. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and curcumin (CURC) are potent antitumor agents that target proliferation, invasion, inflammation, and oxidative stress through distinct mechanisms; however, their clinical utility is limited by poor bioavailability and rapid clearance. This study aimed to develop a bovine serum albumin (BSA) nanoparticle (NP) platform for the co-delivery of ATRA and CURC and to evaluate its antitumor activity in U87-MG GBM cells. Methods: ATRA/CURC-loaded BSA-NPs were synthesized and characterized for particle size, morphology, encapsulation efficiency, and drug release behavior. Cytotoxic and antimigratory effects were assessed in U87-MG cells using real-time xCELLigence proliferation and migration assays, while apoptosis was evaluated by Annexin V/PI staining and flow cytometry at 24, 48, and 72 h. Results: The combination NPs exhibited a mean particle size of 154.7 nm and an encapsulation efficiency 99%, both favorable for BBB permeability. Compared with single-drug formulations, ATRA-CURC-BSA–NPs produced the most pronounced suppression of cell proliferation and the strongest, most sustained inhibition of migration. Apoptosis assays revealed a time-dependent shift from early to late apoptosis, with the combination treatment yielding the highest apoptotic fraction at 72 h, substantially exceeding single-agent groups. Conclusion: Co-delivery of ATRA and CURC via BSA nanoparticles enhances antiproliferative, antimigratory, and pro-apoptotic effects in U87-MG GBM cells compared with single-drug delivery. These findings highlight albumin-based co-delivery of ATRA and CURC as a promising strategy to overcome current therapeutic limitations in glioblastoma and provide a rationale for future translational and in vivo investigations. Keywords: glioblastoma; U87-MG; all-trans retinoic acid; curcumin; BSA nanoparticles; drug delivery; apoptosis; cell migration

title: Better Than Hiding: Gliomas Reprogram the Immune System to Disarm Host Defense

affiliations.name: University of Genova
AOM-IRCCS Ospedale policlinico San Martino

bodyParagraphs: Glioma progression is accompanied by profound changes in the interaction between tumor cells and the immune system. However, the mechanisms through which high-grade gliomas escape immune control remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated this process using a PDGF-B-driven murine model in which low-and high-grade stages of gliomagenesis can be experimentally distinguished. The contribution of different lymphocyte populations to glioma surveillance was examined through transplantation and in vivo immune-cell depletion experiments. Tumor–immune interactions were further characterized by transcriptomic profiling and flow cytometry in in vitro co-culture assays. Our findings identified CD4⁺ T lymphocytes as key initiators of the immune response against glioma cells, promoting the recruitment of cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells. Nevertheless, during malignant progression, glioma cells acquired the ability to interfere with this immune response. Compared with their low-grade counterparts, high-grade glioma cells showed decreased expression of genes associated with MHC class II-mediated antigen presentation and reduced interferon signaling. Moreover, they directly impaired cytotoxic immune populations, decreasing the proportion of granzyme B-expressing CD8⁺ T lymphocytes and NK cells through mechanisms requiring cell–cell contact. The immunomodulatory activity of high-grade glioma cells also affected neighboring tumor cells. Indeed, their co-transplantation promoted the engraftment of low-grade glioma cells that were otherwise immunogenic and unable to generate tumors. Collectively, these results indicate that glioma progression does not depend exclusively on tumor-intrinsic mechanisms that allow malignant cells to remain undetected. Instead, high-grade glioma cells actively reshape the immune microenvironment, suppress cytotoxic responses, and establish conditions permissive for tumor growth.

title: Biomimetic Non-lamellar Lipid Nanoplatforms for Targeted Glioblastoma Multiforme Therapy

affiliations.name: LAQV, REQUIMTE, Department of Chemical Sciences, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Porto

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM), classified as a grade 4 tumor by the WHO, is the most common and malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Despite current therapies, recurrence happens in 75-90% of cases and survival is extremely low as patients usually have a median survival time inferior to 15 months and a 5-year survival rate below 5%. Non-lamellar liquid crystalline lipid nanoparticles are a new generation of lipid nanoparticles that self-assemble into cubic or hexagonal structures. These complex internal architectures improve long-term stability and provide both hydrophilic and lipophilic domains that enable the incorporation of diverse therapeutic agents, their protection from degradation and sustained release. In this study, biomimetic non-lamellar nanocarriers with tumor homing capabilities were developed for GBM therapy. The formulations exhibited suitable sizes for brain drug delivery with a good drug encapsulation efficiency. Stability was maintained for at least 3 months upon storage and for 24 h in protein-rich biological media. The nanoplatforms were hemocompatible and a sustained drug release was achieved at pH 7.4 when compared to a free drug solution. Drug-free formulations were cytocompatible in both healthy and GBM cells, while drug-loaded formulations exhibited dose-dependent anti-cancer activity in GBM cells. The nanoparticles exhibited good permeation across an in vitro BBB model and higher cell uptake in GBM than in non-cancer cells, demonstrating the tumor homing ability of the developed nanoplatforms. Overall, the developed biomimetic nanoplatforms show great potential for targeted GBM therapy.
Keywords: glioblastoma multiforme, non-lamellar lipid nanoparticles, brain drug delivery

title: BRD9 inhibition enhances radiotherapy response in glioblastoma by disrupting MYC-driven translational programs

affiliations.name: Koc University School of Medicine
University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom

bodyParagraphs: Radiotherapy (RT) remains a cornerstone of glioblastoma treatment; however, intrinsic and acquired radioresistance severely limit therapeutic efficacy and contribute to tumor recurrence. Adaptive transcriptional and translational programs activated after ionizing radiation (IR) enable tumor cells to survive genotoxic stress. Identifying molecular regulators that can prime GBM cells for enhanced radiation response represents a critical unmet need.

An epigenetic small-molecule library screen (125 compounds) combined with IR (4 Gy) identified bromodomain-containing protein 9 (BRD9) inhibition as a prominent radiosensitizing strategy. Pharmacological inhibition using structurally distinct BRD9 inhibitors and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated BRD9 loss significantly enhanced IR-induced clonogenic death in glioblastoma cells, while non-malignant astrocytes were minimally affected, indicating tumor-selective vulnerability. BRD9 inhibition primed glioblastoma cells for radiotherapy by increasing apoptotic fractions and delaying resolution of γH2AX and 53BP1 foci following irradiation.

Transcriptomic profiling revealed marked downregulation of MYC target genes, ribosomal biogenesis pathways, and translational programs upon BRD9 perturbation. Consistently, global protein synthesis was reduced upon BRD9 inhibition, suggesting that BRD9 activity sustains MYC-dependent translational capacity required for radiation tolerance. Long-term IR-surviving tumor cell populations exhibited elevated BRD9 expression, supporting its role in adaptive radioresistance. Importantly, ectopic MYC overexpression restored clonogenic survival despite BRD9 inhibition, reversing the primed radiosensitive state.
These findings demonstrate that BRD9 inhibition primes glioblastoma cells for radiotherapy by suppressing MYC-driven translation and highlight a promising radiosensitization strategy.

title: Cannabinoid administration as a therapeutic strategy to improve Glioblastoma response to radiotherapy

affiliations.name: Complutense University of Madrid
Instituto de Investigaciones Sanitarias San Carlos (IdISSC)
Instituto de salud Carlos III

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most frequent brain primary tumor and one of the most aggressive cancer types. Standard treatment consists on combined administration of radiotherapy (RT) and temozolomide (TMZ), although GBMs are highly resistant to radio-chemotherapy and patients frequently recur after its administration. These features are partly attributed to Glioma Initiating Cells (GICs), a stem-like tumor cell population that promotes tumor maintenance and relapse.

Cannabinoids, the main active compounds of marijuana, are being investigated as potential therapeutic agents. Previous studies from our group showed that THC (delta-9-tetrahidrocannabinol), alone or combined with CBD (cannabidiol), together with TMZ targets GICs in vitro and strongly reduces GBM xenograft growth in vivo. In addition to these antitumor effects, THC and CBD also protect non-transformed central nervous system cells, particularly astrocytes, from cytotoxic insults.
Here, we analyzed the effects of combined cannabinoid administration (THC:CBD 1:1) and RT on GICs and the glioma microenvironment.

Our results show that THC:CBD (1:1) enhances the inhibitory effects of RT on: (i) GICs proliferation in vitro; and (ii) the ability of GICs to generate murine orthotopic xenografts. Likewise, in vivo treatment with RT + THC:CBD (1:1) decreased the growth of tumor xenografts generated with GICs and enhanced the survival of the animals at a higher extent than individual treatments. Cannabinoids also protected primary astrocyte cultures from RT-induced cytotoxicity. Moreover, THC:CBD (1:1) abolished the ability of conditioned medium from irradiated astrocytes to promote GICs self-renewal capacity and radioresistance. Finally, using CRISPR/Cas9 library screening together with RNA-seq datasets from GBM patients, we identified candidate genes associated with sensitivity or resistance to cannabinoid + RT treatment.
Altogether, these findings support cannabinoid administration as a potential strategy to increase GICs sensitivity to radiotherapy while reducing RT-induced damage in non-transformed glial cells.

title: CBLs -Towards a skull-based T-cell therapy for glioblastoma treatment.

affiliations.name: DKTK Translational Neurooncology at the West German Cancer Center
Department of Neurosurgery and Spine Surgery, University Hospital Essen, Essen, Germany
University Hospital Essen
Department of Applied Computational Cancer Research, IKIM, University Hospital Essen, Essen, Germany.
Department of Neurosurgery and Spine Surgery

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma is among the most pressing unmet medical needs in oncology. Despite maximal safe tumor resection and temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy, the median overall survival remains poor with approximately 18 months.

We recently identified human skull marrow as a previously unrecognized reservoir of tumor-reactive T cells in patients with glioblastoma. CD45+ immune cells recovered from this compartment were predominantly T cells, which we termed Cranial Bone Lymphoids (CBLs). Integrated single cell gene transcriptomic and T-cell receptor profiling revealed frequent tumor-reactive clonotypes and substantial clonal overlap with tumor-infiltrating T-cells. CBLs exhibited a phenotype consistent with preserved functional fitness and sustained repeated ex vivo expansion capacity, supporting their potential for autologous adoptive T-cell therapy.

Here, we report the initial translational steps toward developing CBLs as an autologous advanced therapeutic medicinal product (ATMP) for glioblastoma. We compare workflows for cell isolation and processing, determine ex vivo expansion capacity, and characterize the cellular composition of the resulting products. We further assess CBL-mediated cytotoxic against autologous tumor cells to evaluate its suitability as a product-specific potency readout. These studies address key feasibility parameters for subsequent process standardization and GMP-compliant manufacturing development.
This work provides the basis for advancing CBLs towards a first-in-human, point-of-care cellular immunotherapy for glioblastoma.
body:
Glioblastoma is among the most pressing unmet medical needs in oncology. Despite maximal safe tumor resection and temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy, the median overall survival remains poor with approximately 18 months.

We recently identified human skull marrow as a previously unrecognized reservoir of tumor-reactive T cells in patients with glioblastoma. CD45+ immune cells recovered from this compartment were predominantly T cells, which we termed Cranial Bone Lymphoids (CBLs). Integrated single cell gene transcriptomic and T-cell receptor profiling revealed frequent tumor-reactive clonotypes and substantial clonal overlap with tumor-infiltrating T-cells. CBLs exhibited a phenotype consistent with preserved functional fitness and sustained repeated ex vivo expansion capacity, supporting their potential for autologous adoptive T-cell therapy.

Here, we report the initial translational steps toward developing CBLs as an autologous advanced therapeutic medicinal product (ATMP) for glioblastoma. We compare workflows for cell isolation and processing, determine ex vivo expansion capacity, and characterize the cellular composition of the resulting products. We further assess CBL-mediated cytotoxic against autologous tumor cells to evaluate its suitability as a product-specific potency readout. These studies address key feasibility parameters for subsequent process standardization and GMP-compliant manufacturing development.

This work provides the basis for advancing CBLs towards a first-in-human, point-of-care cellular immunotherapy for glioblastoma.

title: CDKN2A loss defines a MAPK/RB signaling dependency in BRAF-wildtype GBM and CDK4/6+MEK dual inhibition overcome adaptive resistance

programme.programmeTitle: Beyond oncogenic mutations: identifying actionable vulnerabilities in BRAF-wt glioblastoma resistance

affiliations.name: CNR -Istituto di Neuroscienze
Humanitas Research Hospital
University of Pittsburgh Medical Center Hillman Cancer Center

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains incurable despite aggressive therapeutic approaches. The MAPK pathway is a conserved, MGMT methylation-agnostic, and subtype-independent feature of GBM. In oncology, MAPK inhibition has been clinically restricted, in combination with dabrafenib, to BRAF-mutant patients, yet responses have remained transient because of adaptive resistance mechanisms. In GBM, clinical evaluation of MAPK inhibition has largely been confined to the rare subset of BRAF-mutant tumors (<5%), leaving its therapeutic potential in BRAF-wt disease largely unexplored. By integrating functional screening across a molecularly heterogeneous panel of patient-derived GBM stem-like cell (GSC; n=10; IDH-wt, BRAF-wt) with patient-derived orthotopic xenograft (PDX), we investigated the efficacy of MEK inhibition using trametinib. Trametinib induced dose-dependent suppression of proliferation and self-renewal in most GSCs, whereas a subset exhibited reduced sensitivity. Intrinsic trametinib sensitivity perfectly segregated with CDKN2A status: all sensitive GSC models harbored CDKN2A-deletion, whereas all resistant models retained intact-CDKN2A. Mechanistic studies included cell-cycle analysis, 3D gliomasphere assays, protein profiling, LC-MS/MS drug quantification, and loss-of-function validation using shRNA. Upon MEK inhibition, CDKN2A-deleted GSCs underwent robust Rb-dependent G1 arrest. In contrast, CDKN2A-intact cells failed to establish effective trametinib-dependent cell-cycle blockade. Silencing CDKN2A in resistant, Rb-intact GSCs was sufficient to enhance trametinib sensitivity. In CDKN2A-deleted PDX model, a ten-days trametinib treatment delayed tumor growth and extended survival by approximately 19 days (p<0.05, +17.4%). Prolonged trametinib exposure in-vitro induced adaptive resistance characterized by Rb reactivation and increased AKT signaling. In-vivo, combining trametinib with the brain-penetrant CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib effectively overcame adaptive resistance, significantly extending survival compared with monotherapy (p<0.0001, +41.5%). These findings identify CDKN2A-loss as predictive biomarker of MEK-inhibition response in BRAF-wt GBM, revealing a previously unrecognized MAPK/Rb signaling vulnerability. Adaptive resistance can be overcome through combined CDK4/6 and MEK inhibition, providing a rationale for a new strategy in CDKN2A-deleted BRAF-wt GBM. *Patent evaluation pending; embargo requested until mid-september

title: Cellular Migratory Scaling Stratifies Glioblastoma Survival: PTEN Amino Acid Substitutions as Pro-Invasive Drivers

affiliations.name: Fondazione Pisana per la Scienza
Radiotherapy, Istituto Oncologico Veneto, Padova, Italy
5 Department of Surgical, Oncological and Gastroenterological Sciences (DiSCOG), University of Padova, Padova, Italy
Spedali Riuniti di Livorno, Livorno, Italy
North Texas University, Denton, USA
Liceo Scientifico Statale “C. De Giorgi”, Lecce, Italy

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GB) infiltration is traditionally quantified by kinetic metrics such as speed or distance, which often fail to capture the strategic nature of tumor spreading. In this study, we hypothesized that "migratory efficiency", the mathematical ability of a cell to optimize environmental exploration, serves as a superior predictor of aggressiveness and reflects a distinct molecular landscape. Using cell live imaging on 30 patient-derived GB primary cultures (IDH-WT) to track 4,137 individual trajectories, we applied Diffusion Entropy Analysis (DEA) to calculate the Delta Scaling parameter (d), a scale-invariant metric of motion. This framework allowed us to stratify tumors into Low (L), Medium (M), and High (H) motility groups based on their exploratory efficiency. Our results demonstrate that high d scaling (H) identifies a "highly efficient" phenotype characterized by structured, super-diffusive movement, which directly correlates with significantly shorter patient survival. Multi-omic analysis revealed that Group H is uniquely enriched in PTEN mutations (75% vs. 8% in Group L). Specifically, PTEN amino-acid substitution (AA) carriers in an expanded cohort (n=50) exhibited a dismal median survival of 6.7 months, significantly shorter than both PTEN wild-type cases (16.6 months, p=0.01) and those with canonical truncating (Ter) mutations (14.7 months, p=0.03). Notably, while complete PTEN loss (Ter) showed no significant survival difference from wild-type, the presence of specific AA substitutions significantly worsened the clinical prognosis.Our study demonstrates that migratory efficiency is a powerful predictor of GB prognosis. We provide evidence for a critical paradigm shift: while PTEN loss is a genomic hallmark, specific residual missense mutations correlate with a highly efficient invasive program. This suggests that in the context of habitual gene loss, these alterations may act as pro-invasive or oncogenic drivers, worsening the clinical scenario far beyond the effects of canonical PTEN truncation, offering novel, actionable therapeutic targets for glioblastoma and potentially other PTEN-deficient cancers.

title: Characterisation of calcium active tumor microtube networks in diffuse midline glioma in multiple models

affiliations.name: University Hospital Heidelberg
Hector Institute for Translational Brain Research

bodyParagraphs: BACKGROUND: Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is an aggressive and resistant paediatric-type high-grade glioma. Its growth is influenced in part by neuronal activity and related signalling pathways. In glioblastoma, tumor microtubes (TMs), long cellular extensions, interconnect tumour cells to dense networks. Within these networks, pacemaker-like cells trigger hierarchical rhythmic calcium signalling. This connectivity and communication drive tumour growth and resistance to standard-of-care treatments. However, it is not yet fully understood whether DMGs share these same connective and communicative features. METHODS: Using several patient-derived DMG cell lines, we examined TM-based cell networks across a range of model systems — 2D monolayers, spheroids, co-cultures with iPSC-derived human cortical organoids, and mouse xenografts — and confirmed key findings in human tumour tissue. Immunostaining, live calcium imaging, and two-photon in vivo microscopy were used to characterise the structure and activity of these networks. RESULTS: Nestin-positive TMs forming tumor cell networks were consistently identified in DMG across cell cultures, xenograft models, and patient specimens. Network morphology varied among different patient-derived lines, differing in TM length, branching patterns, and proximity to blood vessels. Distinct morphological types resembled radial glia, neurons, perivascular cells, and OPCs across experimental settings. Observing DMG invasion in vivo over multiple weeks using two-photon microscopy showed single-cell infiltration patterns similar to neuronal migration and invasion patterns seen in glioblastoma. Calcium imaging in vitro and in vivo revealed calcium activity within DMG networks including waves and repeated rhythmic bursts, supporting functional connections between tumor cells. CONCLUSIONS: This work characterises TM-driven network architecture and calcium signalling activity in DMG across diverse experimental models, suggesting these networks could serve as future therapeutic targets. The ability to observe these processes directly in vivo offers a valuable tools of studying and manipulating DMG biology in the living brain.

title: Characterization of F3 (Tissue Factor) Expression and Its Role in Angiogenesis Within Glioblastoma Stem Cells

authors.name: María de los Ángeles Marqués Torrejón

affiliations.name: Universitat Jaume I
Hospital Universitario y Politécnico La Fe de Valencia

bodyParagraphs: Background: Glioblastoma (GB) is a highly vascularized brain tumor characterized by intense angiogenesis, heavily driven by Glioblastoma Stem Cells (GSCs). Tissue Factor (F3) is known to be overexpressed in GB, yet its precise mechanistic role in GSCmediated angiogenesis remains to be fully elucidated. Objective: This study aims to investigate the biological role of F3 expression in GSCs, evaluate its downstream angiogenic network, and determine its direct influence on endothelial cell angiogenic capacity. Methods: To dissect the underlying molecular mechanisms, we established an in vitro knockout (KO) model for F3 in GSCs. Transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify altered angiogenic pathways, followed by qPCR and Western blot analyses to specifically validate the expression of key factors, including VEGFA and F3. Additionally, the functional impact on endothelial cells was evaluated using conditioned media from F3-KO and wild-type GSCs, combined with EdU (5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine) proliferation assays to assess endothelial cell turnover. Results: Transcriptomic data and molecular validation via qPCR and Western blot confirmed the successful depletion of F3 and revealed a significant downregulation of major pro-angiogenic factors, most notably VEGFA, in F3-KO GSCs compared to wildtype controls. Functionally, endothelial cells exposed to conditioned media from F3-KO GSCs exhibited a significantly reduced angiogenic capacity. This impairment was molecularly characterized by a distinct decrease in EdU-positive endothelial cells, indicating a robust suppression of endothelial cell proliferation and cell cycle progression in the absence of GSC-derived F3. Conclusion: These results demonstrate that F3 plays a fundamental role in the basic mechanisms governing GSC-induced angiogenesis by regulating key pro-angiogenic players like VEGFA. Knockout of F3 downregulates crucial signaling pathways and directly impairs endothelial proliferation, highlighting F3 as a key molecular orchestrator of the vascular microenvironment in GB.

title: Characterization of ZBTB18 C-terminal short form function in glioblastoma

affiliations.name: University of Insubria
Medical Center-University of Freiburg

bodyParagraphs: Zinc finger and BTB domain-containing protein 18 (ZBTB18) is a key player in both normal nervous system development and cancer, where it behaves as a tumor suppressor and negative regulator of glioblastoma (GBM) mesenchymal genes. ZBTB18 is cleaved by the calpain 2 (CAPN2) protease, which generates two functionally different fragments (SF-Nte and SF-Cte), SF-Nte acquiring oncogenic functions. However, whether the SF-Cte still retains ZBTB18 tumor suppression function needs to be determined. Here, we have characterized the regulation of ZBTB18 SF-Cte and investigated its function. Our preliminary data suggest that ZBTB18 SF-Cte levels are low due to protein instability. Interestingly, RNAseq data suggest that ZBTB18 SF-Cte retains, at least partly, ZBTB18 suppressive function in tumor. Whether new protein interactions and/or cellular activities are gained is a matter of investigation. Attempts to decipher ZBTB18 SF-Cte interactome suggested the interaction with proteins involved in its degradation. Further investigation of ZBTB18 SF-Cte function and regulation will be important to understand whether targeting key ZBTB18 SF-Cte regulators to increase its stability, could be a therapeutic option to treat glioblastoma.

bodyParagraphs: Background – Despite therapeutic advances, glioblastoma (GBM) remains incurable, partly due to its extensive cellular and molecular heterogeneity. The mesenchymal (MES) phenotype, in particular, is associated with aggressive features, inflammatory signaling, and an immune-enriched microenvironment. Although the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway has been implicated in GBM, its association with subgroup-specific GBM stem cell states, its inter-and intra-tumor heterogeneity, and its functional relevance in patient-derived models remain poorly defined.

Methods – Patient-derived GBM stem cells (GSCs) were cultured in vitro and used for xenograft generation. Kynurenine pathway components were evaluated by immunohistochemistry and western blot, while functional perturbation was performed using shRNA-mediated silencing. The effect of silencing was assessed in vitro by functional assays and in vivo using intracranial NSG xenografts that were longitudinally monitored by MRI. Bioinformatic cross-cohort analyses were performed on public bulk RNA-seq, sc/snRNA-seq, and spatial transcriptomic GBM datasets.

Results – Untargeted metabolomics of proneural and MES GSC-derived xenografts identified kynurenine accumulation as a prominent feature of the MES ones, with TDO2 showing the clearest MES-associated expression among kynurenine-producing enzymes. Across independent GBM cohorts, TDO2 progressively tracked MES identity although displaying marked inter-tumor and intra-tumor heterogeneity. Single-cell and spatial analyses localized TDO2 to specific MES-like malignant states and vascular-associated niches characterized by inflammatory programs. Functionally, TDO2 silencing in MES GSCs significantly impaired tumor growth.

Conclusions – Our findings refine the role of TDO2 in GBM, highlighting it as a candidate MES-associated metabolic vulnerability with functional relevance in patient-derived orthotopic models. Its marked inter-tumor, intra-tumor, and spatial heterogeneity suggests that TDO2 is associated with specific tumor states and niches, rather than representing a universal GBM feature. This heterogeneity may therefore inform patient stratification for future TDO2-targeted approaches.

title: Chromatin Deregulation in Glioblastoma and Applications for Liquid Biopsies

affiliations.name: University of Essex

bodyParagraphs: My project investigates chromatin dynamics in glioblastoma and their application to cell-free DNA (cfDNA) based diagnostics using liquid biopsies. I examine differences in nucleosome positioning between glioblastoma patients and healthy individuals, focusing on dyad position, occupancy, and stability, and on their association with epigenetic modifications. This approach aims to improve understanding of genome organisation and identify disease-associated genomic regions. Plasma-derived cfDNA provides a minimally invasive alternative to tissue biopsies, which are often risky in glioblastoma. It enables real-time monitoring of tumour-associated genetic and epigenetic changes, supporting assessment of disease progression and treatment response. Given the high recurrence rate of glioblastoma, cfDNA analysis is particularly valuable for detecting minimal residual disease and early relapse. The project also investigates tumour heterogeneity by comparing cfDNA-derived signals with those obtained from tissue-based biopsies. Additionally, I develop machine learning models using cfDNA-derived features for glioblastoma classification, creating diagnosis frameworks with potential applications beyond this cancer type. Overall, this research integrates genomic and computational methods to advance non-invasive cancer diagnostics and personalised medicine in glioblastoma.

title: CIITA-mediated MHC-II expression in glioblastoma unveil MHC-II-bound tumor-associated peptides for protective anti-tumor vaccination

affiliations.name: Laboratories of General Pathology and Immunology "Giovanna Tosi"
University of Laussane, Ludwig Cancer Research Center, Laussane, Switzerland

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults and remains largely incurable. Peptide vaccination is a promising immunotherapeutic strategy, but most clinical approaches target MHC-I–restricted antigens to stimulate CD8⁺ T cells, with limited benefit. We previously showed that CIITA-mediated MHC-II expression in GL261 glioblastoma cells induces tumor rejection or growth retardation and durable CD4⁺ T-cell–mediated protection. Here, we used high-throughput immunopeptidomics to characterize MHC-II ligands from murine glioma cell lines (GL261, CT2A, SB28) and their CIITA-transfected counterparts. CIITA robustly induced MHC-II surface expression, enabling identification of over 8,000 unique MHC-II–bound peptides per CIITA-expressing line. Comparative analysis identified a shared core of 5,559 peptides from 1,109 source proteins across all models. Cross-species comparison of GL261-CIITA with CIITA-expressing human GBM cell lines identified 225 conserved source proteins. Five glioblastoma-associated proteins were prioritized, yielding seven candidate MHC-II peptides for immunogenicity testing. C57BL/6 mice immunized with the peptide pool plus CpG adjuvant developed peptide-specific ex vivo IFN-γ responses, with peptides 1, 2, and 4 showing strongest immunogenicity. In an orthotopic GL261 model, these peptides induced antigen-specific antitumor immunity. Complete protection was observed in 30%, 40%, and 20% of mice vaccinated with peptides 1, 2, and 4, respectively. At six months after tumor implantation, survival was 50% (5/10), 30% (3/10), and 20% (2/10), respectively; all CpG-only controls died by day 23. In tumor-bearing mice, peptides 2 and 4 significantly reduced tumor size versus CpG alone, a nonimmunogenic control peptide, or an unrelated immunogenic peptide. All immunogenic peptides increased intratumoral CD3⁺ T-cell infiltration; peptide 2 increased CD4⁺ infiltration, while peptides 2 and 4 promoted CD8⁺ recruitment. Peptide 2 protection required both T-cell subsets, as in vivo depletion of either CD4⁺ or CD8⁺ T cells abolished efficacy. These findings identify conserved glioma-associated MHC-II peptides and support CD4⁺ T-cell–targeted peptide vaccination for GBM.

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric brain tumors remain the leading cause of cancer-related death in children, with poor outcomes driven largely by high-grade glioma (HGG), for which 5-year survival remains below 20% despite standard-of-care multimodal therapy. We previously demonstrated promising clinical activity of GD2-directed CAR T cells in diffuse midline glioma (DMG) harboring H3K27M alterations, where the histone H3 mutation drives high, uniform GD2 expression. In H3 wildtype (H3wt) HGG, however, GD2 expression is more heterogeneous, limiting patient eligibility for current GD2-targeted approaches. We therefore sought to identify complementary ganglioside targets in H3wt HGG.

Analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from 624 HGG samples identified heterogeneous expression of B4GALNT1, the enzyme that converts precursor GD3 to GD2, as a key bottleneck for GD2 abundance in H3wt tumors. Immunohistochemistry in an independent cohort (n=20) confirmed marked spatial heterogeneity of B4GALNT1 protein expression. Using both immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry on patient samples, we found that reduced B4GALNT1 expression in GD2-low tumors was associated with compensatory accumulation of GD3.

To investigate the underlying biology, we correlated GD2 and B4GALNT1 levels with transcriptomic programs in bulk and single-cell RNA-seq datasets from primary H3wt HGG patients. Higher B4GALNT1/GD2 expression was associated with a neuronal progenitor-like cell state, whereas lower B4GALNT1 expression correlated with a mesenchymal program.

To overcome GD2 heterogeneity, we engineered and optimized a bispecific CAR T-cell construct capable of recognizing and eliminating tumor cells expressing either GD2 or GD3. Both antigens have been clinically targeted with favorable safety signals, and staining of normal tissues revealed no major overlapping expression. Together, these findings support dual GD2/GD3 targeting as a strategy to overcome antigen heterogeneity in H3wt HGG and expand ganglioside-directed CAR T-cell therapy to additional pediatric brain tumor patients.

bodyParagraphs: Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) harboring the H3K27M mutation is one of the most aggressive pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGGs), with a dismal prognosis and no effective targeted therapies. The H3K27M mutation disrupts histone H3 methylation and acetylation, leading to widespread epigenetic dysregulation that alters gene expression and protein translation. Here, we sought to identify a targeted combination therapy exploiting these disease-specific vulnerabilities.

An epigenetic drug library screen, followed by combination and synergy screening, identified the combination of a CDK9 inhibitor (CDK9i) and a BET inhibitor (BETi) as the most potent therapeutic strategy for H3K27M DMG. High-content imaging of 3D tumoroids derived from H3K27M, H3 wild-type (WT), and H3G34V pHGG models, together with a non-malignant control, demonstrated significantly greater cytotoxicity of the CDK9i-BETi combination in H3K27M DMG than in the other models. Furthermore, the combination showed additive or synergistic effects with ionizing radiation, supporting its integration with current standard-of-care treatment.

Mechanistically, CDK9 inhibition suppressed translation and reduced MCL1 expression, while BET inhibition downregulated the expression of MYC, and E2F and MYC target genes. Combined treatment selectively induced replication stress in H3K27M cells, as evidenced by increased RPA32 phosphorylation, whereas this effect was markedly less pronounced in H3 WT models. These molecular changes culminated in robust apoptosis in H3K27M DMG cells in vitro. In vivo, the combination significantly reduced tumor burden in zebrafish early larvae xenografted with H3K27M DMG cells but showed limited efficacy against H3 WT and H3G34V tumors.

Together, these findings demonstrate that combined CDK9 and BET inhibition selectively targets H3K27M DMG by suppressing translation and inducing replication stress, ultimately triggering apoptosis. This therapeutic strategy warrants further investigation as a promising candidate for clinical translation in children with H3K27M DMG.

title: Comprehensive analysis of TERT promoter methylation in glioblastoma: associations with molecular features, expression, and survival

affiliations.name: Paul-Flechsig-Institute of Neuropathology, University Hospital Leipzig
Department of Neurosurgery, University Hospital Leipzig
University Clinic of Neurosurgery, University Hospital Jena

bodyParagraphs: While TERT promoter mutations are a well-known molecular feature of glioblastoma, the relevance of TERT promoter methylation remains unclear. Recent studies suggest that TERT promoter methylation is associated with survival in other malignancies. Yet, a comprehensive analysis of TERT promoter methylation and its potential molecular and clinical relevance in glioblastoma is missing. We analyzed 301 glioblastomas from three public datasets (TCGA, GSE195684, GSE60274) and 121 cases from our diagnostic routine. Mutational status, including TERT promoter mutations, MGMT promoter status and copy number variation (CNV) profiles were assessed. Beta values of TERT promoter–associated CpG sites were extracted from Illumina 450k and EPICv1 arrays. TERT promoter methylation was compared with normal brain tissue using GSE90496. TERT RNA expression (TCGA) was correlated with promoter methylation using Spearman’s rank correlation. Differential methylation was analyzed with limma, and survival with survminer. In-house data showed no significant correlation between TERT promoter mutations and methylation, but a trend toward cg11625005 hypermethylation in TERT wild-type tumors. Using Spearman’s rank correlation TERT locus CNV moderately negatively correlated with methylation at cg7380026 (ρ = −0.2) and cg23250191 (ρ = −0.2). TERT promoter CpG sites were significantly differentially methylated compared to normal brain tissue. In TCGA data, methylation of cg10896616 (ρ = 0.4, adj. p = < 0.05), cg17166338 (ρ = 0.3, adj. p < 0.05), and cg26006951 (ρ = 0.3, adj. p < 0.05) positively correlated with TERT expression. Methylation of cg10896616 was associated with overall survival in a multivariate Cox regression model adjusted for MGMT status, age, and sex (HR = 1.1, p < 0.05). Differential methylation using cg10896616 as a continuous variable shows gene enrichments in cancer associated pathways, e.g. MAPK, mTOR and Wnt pathway. TERT promoter methylation has potentially relevant biological and clinical implications in glioblastoma and may improve diagnostic precision and understanding of tumor biology.

title: Convergent Physics-Guided and Deep Learning Analyses Reveal a Common Prognostic Motility Axis in Glioblastoma

affiliations.name: Fondazione Pisana per la Scienza
North Texas University, Denton, USA
Liceo Scientifico Statale “C. De Giorgi”, Lecce, Italy
Spedali Riuniti di Livorno, Livorno, Italy

bodyParagraphs: Background: Cell motility drives glioblastoma (GBM) invasion, but biomarkers linking migration dynamics to patient outcome are lacking. We investigated whether two computational frameworks identify a common prognostic dimension. Methods: Single-cell trajectories from 27 primary IDH1-wild-type GBM cultures were monitored by time-lapse imaging. Data were analyzed using a physics-guided framework to extract population-level descriptors, including the mean squared displacement (MSD) scaling exponent α, defining the diffusion regime. Concurrently, a neural network autoencoder compressed 50-frame trajectory windows into a two-dimensional latent space, clustered (K-means, silhouette-validated) into three reproducible cell-level phenotypes. Per-line phenotype composition was correlated with α and overall survival using multivariate Cox regression and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Results: Physics-guided analysis identified α as the only independent predictor of survival (p=0.023), with mortality risk increasing nonlinearly above α=1.04. Independently, autoencoder-derived phenotype composition strongly correlated with α (r=-0.56, p=0.004): the low-motility "Confined" phenotype was associated with longer overall survival (log-rank p=0.005), whereas high-motility "Exploratory" phenotypes were associated with shorter survival (p=0.025). Conclusions: Two independent approaches converged on the same biophysical axis: low-motility, subdiffusive dynamics marked a favorable clinical phenotype, whereas high-motility, superdiffusive dynamics identified a high-risk phenotype. These findings support cell-resolved dynamical profiling as a robust candidate prognostic biomarker in GBM.

title: Deciphering aging-associated drivers of glioblastoma biology at the tumor core and border

affiliations.name: Charité -University Hospital Berlin
Berlin Institute for Medical Systems Biology
Berlin Institute of Health at Charité
Owkin Inc.
Vivantes Klinikum Neukölln

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GB), IDH-wildtype, is an age-related disease peaking around age 65, yet the impact of aging on its biology remains poorly understood.

Here, we present a spatially resolved multi-omics framework to characterize age-associated differences in GB. We analyzed 142 FFPE samples from 112 primary GB patients (36–86 years), including 74 patients from the MOSAIC consortium, using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, bulk DNA methylation profiling, targeted/whole-exome sequencing, and -in a subset -spatial transcriptomics. Histologically selected regions captured the full spatial heterogeneity of GB, including 30 samples from normal-appearing peritumoral brain. To establish a healthy aging reference, we profiled 16 cortical surgery samples from non-oncological patients (35–100 years) and integrated these data with published single-cell brain RNA-seq atlases (700 patients) spanning the human lifespan.

Overall, transcriptomic differences between younger and older patients were modest compared with variation driven by spatial heterogeneity, epigenetic subtype (RTK1, RTK2, mesenchymal), driver mutations, and clinical factors such as preoperative dexamethasone treatment, underscoring the need for carefully controlled age-group comparisons.

Preliminary analyses indicate fewer OPC-and NPC-like malignant cells in older patients, accompanied by reduced non-malignant OPCs. In contrast, GPC-like tumor cells increased with age independently of EGFR amplification. Among non-malignant cells, astrocytes exhibited a more reactive A1-like phenotype, consistent with healthy aging, while microglia shifted from homeostatic to immunosuppressive transcriptional programs. Notably, age-related differences diminished toward the tumor core, where aging-associated signatures were most strongly expressed, suggesting convergence through tumor-driven activation of pathways normally upregulated during physiological aging.

To quantify aging-associated processes in GB relative to healthy controls, ongoing analyses integrate transcriptomic, epigenetic, and radiological aging clocks. Finally, we evaluate the clinical relevance of these processes by correlating them with survival and radiographic endpoints.
Together, this study provides a comprehensive view of how aging shapes the glioblastoma ecosystem and may guide age-adapted therapeutic strategies.

title: Deciphering Ceramide Biosynthesis as a Metabolic Dependency in MYC-Driven Group 3 Medulloblastoma

affiliations.name: IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute and Vita-Salute San Raffaele University
IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute and Vita-Salute San Raffaele University.
University of Milan

bodyParagraphs: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant paediatric brain tumour, classified into four molecular subgroups with distinct biology and prognosis. Among these, MYC-amplified Group 3 MB (MB Grp3) represents one of the highest-risk variants, with 5-year survival below 40% despite aggressive multimodal treatment that leads to severe long-term neurocognitive and endocrine sequelae. Metabolic reprogramming has emerged as a key cancer hallmark driving tumour progression and treatment resistance, making subgroup-specific metabolic vulnerabilities a promising, largely unexplored therapeutic strategy in high-risk MB. To this end, we profiled mouse models of Myc-driven and Shh TP53-mutant MB by bulk RNA-sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. Myc-amplified MB Grp3 displayed higher lipid accumulation, predominantly sphingolipids (SL), than Shh p53mut MBs and controls. Metabolic enzymes were characterized across complementary human models, including patient-derived orthotopic xenografts (PDOXs), FFPE specimens, PDOX-derived MB stem cells (MBSCs) and their xenografts, and MB human cell lines. Pharmacological MYC inhibition (10058-F4) and radioactive metabolic flux assays were used to probe pathway regulation and activity. The ceramide (CER) biosynthetic metabolism emerged as a distinguishing feature, with Myc MB-restricted upregulation of enzymes like SPTLC1, CERS2, and CERS4. CERS4 was the most robust, subgroup-specific isoform, and its expression was selectively reduced upon pharmacological MYC inhibition in human MYC MB Grp3 cells, but not in SHH cells, supporting direct MYC-dependent regulation. Metabolic flux assays in human MBSCs confirmed enhanced CER synthesis and conversion into complex CER species in MYC-versus SHH-driven cells. As CER can act as either pro-apoptotic or pro-survival signal depending on its downstream fate, we confirmed that pharmacologically shifting this balance selectively impairs MYC MBSC viability, supporting the functional relevance of the pathway. These data identify CER biosynthesis, and CERS4 in particular, as a MYC-regulated, subgroup-selective metabolic dependency in high-risk MB Grp3, revealing novel druggable vulnerabilities for precision therapy in this aggressive paediatric tumor.

title: Defining Epigenetic Vulnerabilities and Response Programs in IDH-Mutant Gliomas

programme.programmeTitle: Defining Epigenetic Vulnerabilities and Response Programs in IDH-Mutant Gliomas

affiliations.name: Koc University School of Medicine

bodyParagraphs: IDH-mutant gliomas are epigenetically dysregulated tumors with limited therapeutic options at recurrence. Identifying chromatin-regulatory dependencies specific to the IDH-mutant context may reveal new treatment strategies. Using a chromatin-focused CRISPR/Cas9 knockout library screen, we identified RBBP7 as a potential IDH-mutant-specific dependency. Functional validation and RNA sequencing were performed in isogenic IDH-wildtype and IDH-mutant glioma cells and extended to 3D patient-derived IDH-mutant glioma stem-like models, revealing context-dependent effects of RBBP7 loss on proliferation, differentiation, and inflammatory programs. In parallel, an epigenetic drug screen identified KDM6A/6B as candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities. Following pharmacological confirmation, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated single-and double-knockout of KDM6A and KDM6B was performed in 3D patient-derived IDH-mutant glioma stem-like models. Functional characterization and RNA sequencing defined the transcriptional and phenotypic consequences of KDM6A/6B loss. Comparative analysis of RBBP7 and KDM6A/6B perturbation signatures is ongoing to determine whether these vulnerabilities converge on shared response pathways. To extend translational relevance, patient-derived glioma organoid models are being established, and perturbation signatures will be integrated with public glioma datasets, including TCGA, CGGA, and GLASS, to assess clinical correlates such as recurrence and progression. Together, this work supports the identification of epigenetic dependencies in IDH-mutant glioma and provides a framework to understand how chromatin perturbations reshape tumor cell states, with implications for future therapeutic targeting.

title: Development of a multimodal platform for the characterization of glioblastoma circulating tumor cells using FLIM Analysis

affiliations.name: Fondazione Pisana per la Scienza
Spedali Riuniti di Livorno, Livorno, Italy

bodyParagraphs: Background: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is an aggressive malignancy where liquid biopsy, specifically circulating tumor cell (CTC) isolation, offers a promising non-invasive tool for longitudinal disease monitoring. However, capturing GBM CTCs remains challenging due to their rarity and lack of epithelial markers. This study develops a workflow combining microfluidic enrichment, nanostructured slide immobilization, and Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) to phenotypically and metabolically characterize GBM CTCs. Methods: The platform was initially validated using a spike-in model of T98G GBM cells mixed with healthy lymphocytes. The cell suspension was deposited onto Tethis slides prior to immunofluorescence (IF) staining using Cell-Surface Vimentin (CSV) as the tumor marker and CD45 for lymphocytes. Crucially, this pipeline has already been successfully applied to clinical samples: whole blood from GBM patients was enriched via the Parsortix system, immobilized on Tethis slides, and stained for CSV and CD45. Extracted cells were quantified using an Olympus confocal microscope and analyzed via autofluorescence FLIM for metabolic profiling and DAPI-FLIM for chromatin conformation. Results: Spike-in experiments demonstrated efficient cell adhesion on the Tethis platform. IF staining successfully differentiated T98G tumor cells from the surrounding CD45+ background. Real patient sample experiments using the Parsortix system confirmed the effectiveness of the protocol for CTC isolation and identification. Preliminary FLIM analyses revealed a unique metabolic signature in tumor cells compared to healthy lymphocytes, while DAPI-FLIM optimization showed distinct variations in chromatin architecture between the two populations. Conclusions: This integrated pipeline successfully couples morphological, phenotypic, and metabolic single-cell analysis. Validated in both spiked models and initial clinical samples, the platform represents a powerful tool for characterizing GBM CTCs and tracking disease progression.

title: Dexamethasone induces immunosuppressive remodeling of the brain tumor microenvironment associated with poor prognosis

programme.programmeTitle: Dexamethasone induces immunosuppressive remodeling of the brain tumor microenvironment associated with poor prognosis

affiliations.name: Charité -University Hospital Berlin
Berlin Institute for Medical Systems Biology
Universitätsklinikum Düsseldorf
Owkin Inc.

bodyParagraphs: Brain tumors patients often develop brain edema which is routinely treated with dexamethasone (DEXA). We previously demonstrated that preoperative DEXA administration is an independent negative prognostic factor in both glioblastoma (GB) and non-small cell lung cancer brain metastases (NSCLCm). Although glucocorticoids are known to suppress inflammatory responses, the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their long-lasting effects on the brain tumor microenvironment remain poorly understood.

To address this question, we analyzed single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from 89 GB, including 74 patients from the MOSAIC consortium, and 30 NSCLCm specimens obtained at primary surgery and stratified samples according to preoperative DEXA exposure (none, short-term, or long-term). To extend the analysis longitudinally, we additionally sequenced 15 matched recurrent tumor samples.

Preliminary analyses identified multiple DEXA-associated immunosuppressive programs in myeloid cells, including upregulation of IL1R2 in neutrophils and CD163 in microglia, accompanied by reduced T-cell activation characterized by decreased IFN-γ signaling and diminished CD40–CD40L interactions. The magnitude of these immunosuppressive signatures correlated with expression of canonical glucocorticoid receptor (GR) target genes, including FKBP5 and ZBTB16. Notably, both baseline GR target gene activity and the transcriptional response to DEXA varied substantially between patients. body:
Brain tumors patients often develop brain edema which is routinely treated with dexamethasone (DEXA). We previously demonstrated that preoperative DEXA administration is an independent negative prognostic factor in both glioblastoma (GB) and non-small cell lung cancer brain metastases (NSCLCm). Although glucocorticoids are known to suppress inflammatory responses, the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their long-lasting effects on the brain tumor microenvironment remain poorly understood.

To address this question, we analyzed single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from 89 GB, including 74 patients from the MOSAIC consortium, and 30 NSCLCm specimens obtained at primary surgery and stratified samples according to preoperative DEXA exposure (none, short-term, or long-term). To extend the analysis longitudinally, we additionally sequenced 15 matched recurrent tumor samples.

Preliminary analyses identified multiple DEXA-associated immunosuppressive programs in myeloid cells, including upregulation of IL1R2 in neutrophils and CD163 in microglia, accompanied by reduced T-cell activation characterized by decreased IFN-γ signaling and diminished CD40–CD40L interactions. The magnitude of these immunosuppressive signatures correlated with expression of canonical glucocorticoid receptor (GR) target genes, including FKBP5 and ZBTB16. Notably, both baseline GR target gene activity and the transcriptional response to DEXA varied substantially between patients. Ongoing studies are investigating whether GR-pathway activation measured in peripheral blood correlates with GR-dependent remodeling of the tumor microenvironment.

Together, these findings provide a potential mechanistic explanation for the adverse clinical effects associated with DEXA treatment in brain tumor patients and suggest that baseline GR activity may serve as a biomarker to guide personalized glucocorticoid therapy.

title: Disrupting Golgi dependent signalling uncovers a Vulnerability in Medulloblastoma stem cells

University of L’Aquila
Sapienza University of Rome
National Research Council (CNR)
University G. D’Annunzio of Chieti

bodyParagraphs: Background: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, which frequently exhibits treatment resistance and recurrence, largely attributed to MB stem cells (MBSCs). Recently, we demonstrated that treatment of MBSCs with Brefeldin A (BFA), an inhibitor of Golgi function, reduces the stem-like phenotype by inducing the proteolytic cleavage of the stem cell marker CD133, thereby impairing its function. However, the limited clinical applicability of BFA has driven the search for structurally related compounds with greater target specificity. Among these, Golgicide A (GCA) has emerged as a potent inhibitor of Golgi function. Based on this rationale, we investigated the effects of GCA on MBSCs.

Methods: G3MB cell lines (D283 and D341) were grown in stem selective medium and treated with GCA for 48 hrs. Stemness and apoptotic proteins and oncogenic signalling levels were assessed by western blotting. Gene expression data were retrieved using R2 genomics platform. Results: GCA impaired the stem-like phenotype of MBSCs by inducing proteolytic cleavage of CD133, reducing the expression of the stemness markers, and significantly decreasing medullosphere formation. Furthermore, GCA triggered apoptotic signaling and inhibited the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. Notably, treatment with GCA also resulted in a marked downregulation of a Golgi-resident protein (Golgi-RP), previously implicated as an oncogenic factor in other tumoral contexts. Bioinformatic analyses further revealed that Golgi-RP is preferentially expressed in Group 3 MB, supporting its potential relevance in MB biology. Conclusions: Our findings identify GCA as a structural and functional analogue of BFA capable of targeting CSC-associated pathways in MB. Modulation of CD133 processing and Golgi-dependent signaling emerges as a promising therapeutic strategy in MB, warranting further preclinical investigation. Building on these findings, an ongoing in silico and in vitro screening of structurally related natural and synthetic products is being conducted using GCA as hit compounds.

title: Dissecting spatial niches and immunological cues in glioblastoma for novel biomarkers and precision therapies

bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by its heterogeneity, which renders standardized treatment largely ineffective, underlining the need for novel patient-tailored combination strategies. HOXA9 and WNT6 are oncogenic factors associated with worse GBM prognosis. HOXA9 and WNT6 have been shown to sustain immunoregulatory roles in various contexts, and in GBM we have found an association between these molecules and several immune-related markers and processes. Thus, we aim to explore HOXA9/WNT6-driven effects on GBM-immune spatial architecture, unveiling potential therapeutic strategies. Materials and Methods: GBM patient samples analyzed by Visium (10X Genomics; Ravi et al., 2022; Tirosh et al., 2024) were used to assess the co-expression of HOXA9/WNT6 with immune cell types. Additionally, GBM patients from TCGA were stratified into HOXA9/WNT6-high and -low groups for differential expression analysis, with selected genes subjected to literature querying and univariate survival analysis. Pharmacologic inhibition of HOXA9 (direct by DB818, indirect by buparlisib) and WNT signaling (E7386) were assessed in four paired HOXA9-and WNT6-modulated cell models. Results: HOXA9/WNT6 show spatial co-expression with multiple immune signatures in GBM, particularly of T cells. HOXA9/WNT6 double-high patients present a downregulation of several genes associated with better survival. In vitro, HOXA9-high cells show greater sensitivity to pharmacologic HOXA9 inhibition. WNT signaling inhibition decreases WNT6-driven aggressiveness in overexpression models and acts synergistically with WNT6 silencing in knockdown models. Conclusions: These findings shed light on the association between HOXA9/WNT6 and GBM immune landscape and suggest their pharmacologic targeting as a potential therapeutic avenue. Importantly, ongoing spatial transcriptomics and combination treatment studies, using co-cultures with hPBMCs and humanized in vivo models, will further explore this axis, potentially contributing toward more effective GBM care.

title: Dissecting the contribution of ZBTB18 and TIP60 complex to the mesenchymal/quiescent state in GBM

affiliations.name: University of Insubria
Medical Center-University of Freiburg

bodyParagraphs: The mesenchymal-like (MES-like) cell state of glioblastoma (GBM) has been associated with its most aggressive features. Single-cell RNAseq studies have revealed that MES-like tumors contain a high proportion of slow-cycling cells, which are responsible for therapy resistance, tumor recurrence and the establishment of the GBM immunosuppressive environment. Interestingly, upon recurrence, a mesenchymal-like shift often occurs. It seems this is, at least partly, caused by quiescent mesenchymal cells (qGBM) that have increased their proliferation rate or exited quiescence. Importantly, qGBM cells also evade immune surveillance, contributing to the establishment of the GBM immunosuppressive environment. We have previously pinpointed Zinc finger and BTB domain-containing protein 18 (ZBTB18) as a transcriptional repressor of mesenchymal genes and a tumor suppressor in GBM. In order to get more insight into ZBTB18-mediated transcriptional repression mechanism, we performed co-immunoprecipitation experiments, followed by mass spectrometry (MS), in brain tumor stem-like cells (BTSC), which express ZBTB18. The analysis revealed that many components of the NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex are putative ZBTB18 interactors. The catalytic subunit KAT5 of this complex has been recently shown to oppose the quiescent state in GBM. Based on previous reports and on our preliminary data, we hypothesize ZBTB18 and NuA4/TIP60 complex interact to regulate the expression of genes important for the mesenchymal/quiescent GBM state. Examination of the acetylation status of histone H4 by ChIPseq in BTSCs revealed a global enrichment of acetylated peaks at genes previously linked to qGBM cells upon both ZBTB18 and KAT5 ko. In particular, our data suggest that ZBTB18 and NuA4/TIP60 complex may inhibit the MES/qGBM state by interfering with TGFB3-mediated gene activation.

title: Effects of Polystyrene Nanoplastics on Neural and Glioblastoma Stem Cells

authors.name: María de los Ángeles Marqués Torrejón

affiliations.name: University Jaume I, Facultat de Ciències de la Salut
University of Tunis El Manar, Faculty of Sciences of Tunis
University Rouen Normandy

bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Micro-and nanoplastics (MNPs) are emerging environmental pollutants with potential health risks, yet their impact on brain tumor progression remains unclear. Given the high proliferative capacity of glioblastoma (GBM), understanding the effect of Polystyrene nanoplastic particles (PS-NPs) on tumor interactions is critical for assessing environmental contributions to cancer biology. Cellular models such as Neural stem cells (NSCs) and glioblastoma stem cells (NPEs), which are key drivers of tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance, provide relevant cellular models for investigating these effects. Methods: Murine adult neural stem cells (NSCs) and glioblastoma stem cells (NPEs) were exposed to varying concentrations of polystyrene nanoplastics (100nm) for 24–72 h. Cell viability was assessed by MTT assay, and fluorescent microscopy was used to examine morphological changes. Ki67, PH3, H2AX, and active Casp3 localization were visualized by immunofluorescence with confocal microscopy. Global proteomic profiling was performed by protein extraction, SDS-PAGE separation, tryptic digestion, and HPLC–MS/MS analysis, followed by protein identification and quantitative analysis. Results: Exposure to PS-NPs induced dose-and time-dependent changes in cell viability. Immunofluorescence analyses revealed differential expression of Ki67, PH3, γH2AX, and cleaved caspase-3 between NPEs and NSCs, indicating that PS-NPs elicit distinct cellular responses in glioblastoma stem cells compared with healthy neural stem cells. Proteomic analysis further identified alterations in proteins associated with neurodegeneration, DNA damage, cell proliferation, and survival pathways. Conclusions: PS-NPs promote pro-proliferative responses in glioblastoma stem cells and may activate molecular pathways that support tumor growth and survival, while promoting neurodegeneration and death in healthy neural stem cells.
Keywords: Polystyrene nanoplastics; glioblastoma stem cells; neural stem cells; tumor growth; neurodegeneration; DNA damage; apoptosis.

bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Glioblastoma (GB) remains one of the most aggressive primary brain tumors despite multimodal treatment approaches. Although microRNA (miRNA)-based replacement therapies hold considerable therapeutic potential, their clinical application is hindered by poor stability, limited tissue penetration, and insufficient tumor-selective delivery. The transferrin receptor CD71, encoded by TFRC, is a key mediator of iron uptake and is highly expressed in metabolically active GB cells, thereby representing a potential endogenous gateway for targeted delivery. Methods: To characterize TFRC distribution within GB tissue, we integrated single-cell reference atlases with spatial transcriptomic analyses. CD71 protein expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry, while miR-139-5p localization was assessed using miRNAscope in matched tumor and adjacent peritumoral regions. miRNA delivery was performed using an engineered humanized ferritin nanocage derived from Archaeoglobus fulgidus and loaded with a PAMAM dendrimer (hFt-NP). Nanoparticle uptake, tissue penetration, miR-139-5p restoration, and biological effects were investigated in patient-derived GB cell cultures and organotypic human cultures (OHCs). Results: TFRC expression was associated with malignant astrocytic, hypoxic, and inflammatory transcriptional programs, with TFRC-high tumor cells preferentially localized within myeloid-rich niches. At the protein level, CD71 was markedly enriched in tumor regions, whereas miR-139-5p expression was predominantly retained in peritumoral areas. hFt-NPs efficiently penetrated OHCs, displayed CD71-associated uptake, restored miR-139-5p levels, reduced Ki-67 positivity, and promoted progressive

cell-cycle arrest. Conclusions: Our findings identify TFRC/CD71-high niches as biologically relevant targets for ferritin-mediated miRNA delivery in GB. In addition, these observations establish patient-derived OHCs as a clinically relevant ex vivo platform for studying nanoparticle penetration, targeted delivery, and therapeutic activity within preserved tumor microenvironmental contexts.

title: Glioblastoma cell-derived APLN acts as a chemoattractant for tumor-associated myeloid cells

affiliations.name: Johannes Kepler University Linz and Kepler University Hospital, Austria
University Hospital, LMU Munich, Munich, Germany
Johannes Kepler University Linz, Austria

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) progression is driven by tumor-induced immunosuppression and the massive accumulation of tumor-associated myeloid cells (TAMs). Consequently, signaling pathways governing myeloid cell tropism represent promising therapeutic targets. We previously showed that the angiogenic factor APLN signals through its receptor APLNR to regulate neovascularization and GBM invasion; additionally, TCGA database analysis revealed that APLNR expression correlates with lymphocyte-mediated immune responses. Here, we investigated the role of the APLN-APLNR axis in GBM-immune cell interactions using primary GBM cells, murine myeloid cells (BV2 and J774), and APLN-knockout mice. Myeloid migration was assessed via Boyden chamber and µ-slide chemotaxis assays. In human GBM xenografts, APLN expression directly correlated with TAM density in both the tumor core and invasive front. We confirmed APLN expression in primary GBM cells and APLNR expression in Iba1-positive TAMs, primary microglia and myeloid cultures. In vitro, GBM-conditioned medium stimulated myeloid cell migration, which was fully abrogated when using APLN-knockdown (AKD) GBM medium. Notably, J774 macrophages only migrated toward APLN after prolonged exposure to GBM-secreted factors, which dynamically upregulated APLNR expression. Our findings identify tumor-derived APLN as a novel myeloid cell chemoattractant that shapes TAM distribution within the GBM microenvironment. Targeting the APLN-APLNR axis represents a promising multi-modal therapeutic strategy to simultaneously inhibit angiogenesis, tumor cell invasion, and immunosuppressive myeloid cell recruitment.

bodyParagraphs: We recently discovered hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in the tumor tissue of patients with the uncurable brain tumor glioblastoma. Here we reveal that a lymphopoietic subpopulation of HSPCs negatively correlates with patient survival and we reveal the underlying cellular mechanism which builds on contact-dependent development of hematopoietic fate in the solid tissue microenvironment. Through prospective and retrospective analysis of two independent clinical cohorts using patient derived tissue and cellular models for spatial and single cell derived analyses, we were able to decipher the instructive role of hematopoietic evolution on tumor cell activity by specific antigen-receptor interactions. In co-culture models and in co-clinical patient-derived tissue samples, we were able to interfere with this interdependency by pharmacological inhibition of the lymphopoietic trajectory, or by the use of tools that induce antibody-dependent cytotoxicity (ADCC). Our results highlight a surprising, yet unrecognized role of intra-tumor hematopoietic trajectories that foster glioblastoma growth. An immediate translational route may be considered that makes use of the availability of clinical grade antibodies in settings of controlled clinical trials.

title: Glioblastoma with diverse oncogenic drivers share translationally relevant vascular elements.

affiliations.name: University Hospital, LMU Munich
