bodyParagraphs: The enormous inter-and intra-individual heterogeneity of glioblastoma (GBM), both on the level of tumor genetics and cellular composition, represents a major caveat for successful clinical management. However, identification of conserved neurodevelopmental pattern within the diverse cellular and genetic landscape of GBM raised hopes for the identification of therapeutic targets with broader impact for this entity. We hypothesized that glioma stem cell (GSC) differentiation may represent another, common evolutionary element in gliomagenesis. We generated a transgenic, lineage-tracing mouse model for GBM in which GSCs are readily identifiable by a fluorescent reporter. Furthermore, the model permits investigating diverse GBM driver mutations generating tumor subsets that differ e.g. in overall survival. Histopathological inspection revealed that the intratumoral vascular pattern also varied among genetically distinct GBM. However, lineage identification of intratumoral vascular mural cells (VMCs) demonstrated that genetically distinct GBM commonly harbored a large population of tumor-derived VMCs (td-VMCs). Orthotopic transplantation of GSCs generated GBM with td-VMCs, but GBM cell-lines did not. Conditional knockout of platelet derived growth factor receptor-B (PDGFRB) in the GBM primordium prevented td-VMC generation, suggesting that td-VMC formation recapitulated a neurodevelopmental process. Lineage ablation of td-VMCs resulted in vascular normalization and increased permeability, while targeting host-derived VMCs had adverse effects. Altogether, we show that td-VMCs have broad therapeutic relevance for genetically diverse GBM and that adjuvant treatments for td-VMCs can overcome therapy resistance imposed by the blood-tumor barrier.

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG), the most common pediatric brain tumors, are predominantly driven by alterations activating the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, leading to oncogene-induced senescence (OIS). Although chemotherapy and MAPK-targeted inhibitors show clinical efficacy, rebound growth and disease progression remain significant challenges in unresectable tumors. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are therapeutic targets in several cancers, including MAPK-driven tumors, but their role in pLGG remains poorly defined. Notably, we found HDAC1 expression to be increased in pilocytic astrocytoma compared with normal cerebellum. Given the clinical availability of HDAC inhibitors, we investigated their anti-tumor activity and their potential as combination partners for established therapies in pLGG.

A panel of clinically relevant HDAC inhibitors was tested in drug sensitivity and combination screens using patient-derived pLGG cell lines harboring KIAA1549::BRAF fusions or BRAF-V600E alterations in proliferation and OIS. Drug responses were assessed using metabolic activity assays, viable cell counts, and caspase-3/7 activity measurements. Synergy was quantified using the Bliss model on the platform SynergyFinder. Effects on gene expression and protein abundance were investigated by qPCR and western blot, respectively.

Several HDAC inhibitors showed anti-tumor activity across pLGG models, with romidepsin and fimepinostat, both targeting class I HDACs including HDAC1, emerging as the most promising compounds active at clinically achievable concentrations. Combination screening identified an in-class synergy between HDAC inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Bliss synergy scores were particularly high in senescent cells, especially in KIAA1549::BRAF fusion models. The combination of romidepsin and trametinib significantly reduced viable cell numbers and induced apoptosis, indicated by increased caspase-3/7 activity. Mechanistically, co-treatment was associated with accumulation of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins BIM and BMF and transcriptional changes consistent with a shift towards a pro-apoptotic state.
In conclusion, HDACi-MEKi co-treatment may represent a novel strategy to improve MAPK-targeted therapy in pLGG, particularly by enhancing the elimination of senescent tumor cells.

title: How dendritic cell maturation instructs leptomeningeal anti-tumor immunity

programme.programmeTitle: How dendritic cell maturation instructs leptomeningeal anti-tumor immunity

affiliations.name: VIB Center for Cancer Biology
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

bodyParagraphs: Metastasis to the cerebrospinal fluid-filled leptomeninges, or leptomeningeal metastasis, is a fatal complication of solid tumors. Multimodal analyses of clinical specimens reveal a substantial inflammatory infiltrate enriched for IFN-γ and its downstream signaling. To dissect and overcome this seemingly futile anti-tumor response, we developed syngeneic lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma models of leptomeningeal metastasis. Transgenic hosts lacking IFN-γ or its receptor fail to control tumor growth, whereas leptomeningeal overexpression of Ifng through a targeted adeno-associated virus system restrains cancer cell growth. Using a suite of transgenic hosts, we show that leptomeningeal T cells generate IFN-γ to recruit and activate peripheral myeloid cells, giving rise to diverse dendritic cell subsets. Independent of antigen presentation, migratory CCR7+ dendritic cells orchestrate the influx, proliferation, and cytotoxic activity of NK cells to control cancer cell growth. While these findings define a leptomeninges-specific IFN-γ circuit, we show that the interferon pathway is preferentially engaged by cDC2 to prime innate immunity, leaving the cDC1 population refractory. We therefore perturbed pathways that selectively license cDC1 maturation, aiming to support the innate, NK cell-centric program with a long-lasting adaptive response.

bodyParagraphs: Background: CAR immune-cell therapies for glioblastoma remain limited by insufficient activity within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and by the lack of human tissue models that preserve tumor–brain interactions. Human organotypic brain slices provide an opportunity to evaluate engineered immune-cell therapies in a structurally preserved human microenvironment containing tumor cells and non-malignant brain-resident populations. Methods: We established a human organotypic glioma-infiltrated brain-slice model by implanting fluorescent patient-derived glioblastoma cells into human cortical slices. Tumor-infiltrated slices were treated with allogeneic PBMC or rapidly generated CAR-PBMC co-electroporated with activating cytokines. Live imaging was used to monitor tumor outgrowth and immune-cell infiltration. Immunofluorescence assessed tumor-cell apoptosis, invasion-associated markers, and preservation of non-malignant brain-cell populations, including neurons, astrocytes, and microglia. Single-cell transcriptomics were used to define tumor-cell states, immune-cell composition, and payload-dependent remodeling of the tumor–immune microenvironment. Results: Cytokine-armored CAR-PBMC infiltrated tumor-bearing human brain slices and reduced glioma outgrowth compared with untreated and mock-PBMC controls (P<0.01). Treatment increased tumor-cell apoptosis, supported by elevated caspase-3 staining (Kruskal–Wallis P = 0.015) and apoptosis-associated transcriptional programs. CAR-PBMC also altered tumor architecture and invasion-associated features, including significant reduction of MMP9 (Kruskal–Wallis P = 0.0070) and a trend toward reduced Vimentin signal. Non-malignant brain-cell populations were broadly preserved, including astrocytes, microglia, and total nuclei. Different cytokine activation CAR-PBMC had different effects on the neuron populations, from not reduction to modest neuronal reduction. Immune profiling revealed distinct payload-dependent remodeling. Cytokine-armored CAR-PBMC promoted cytotoxic activation but were associated with higher activation, proliferation, regulatory, and lower exhaustion-associated signatures in T-cell programs.

Conclusion: Human glioma-infiltrated organotypic brain slices provide a translational platform for evaluating engineered immune-cell therapies within a preserved human tumor–brain microenvironment. Using this model, we show that cytokine-armored CAR-PBMC can restrict glioma growth, induce tumor-cell apoptosis, and reshape the tumor–immune landscape in a payload-specific manner. These findings nominate CAR-PBMC for glioblastoma immunotherapy.

title: Identification and therapeutic targeting of paracrine signaling cues inducing mesenchymal drift of infiltrating glioblastoma

affiliations.name: LMU

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) almost invariably relapse and the recurrent tumor likely derives from invasive tumor cells escaping neurosurgical resection and adjuvant treatment. Interaction of GBM cells with the microenvironment fosters therapy resistance, but we lack detailed knowledge on the protumorigenic signaling cues in the invasive zone. Here, we used an orthotopic mouse model to monitor the transcriptomic states of genetically engineered, human GBM cells and observed that acquisition of a “mesenchymal” (MES) state in the infiltrative margin promotes chemoresistance. Also, we identified parenchymal cells inducing mesenchymalization of invasive GBM cells. This was achieved with engineered tumor cells that labeled neighboring, microenvironmental cells promoting mesenchymal drift in GBM. Using this model, we confirmed a predominant role for myeloid cells in initiating mesenchymalization of the tumor core. However, in the tumor invasive margin other parenchymal cells had higher capacity for the induction of MES-GBM and in particular mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC) were identified as powerful inducers of mesenchymal shifts. In vitro gene expression analysis revealed that MSCs modulate tumor cells through TGF-β induced phosphorylation of SMAD2/3 and increased ID1 expression. In in vivo experiments we investigated the interaction of MSCs with invasive GBM cells. We corroborated that invading GBM cells neighboring with MSCs acquired a MES state, while in other infiltrating GBM cells the proneural subtype dominated. Activity of the pSMAD2/3 and ID1 pathways directly correlated with mesenchymalization of GBM. Combinatorial application of the TGF-β Blocker Galunisertib (GAL) together with temozolomide attenuated pSMAD2/3-and ID1-signaling and tumor mesenchymal drift. Notably, the number of gamma H2A.X positive, infiltrating GBM cells was strongly increased after coapplication of GAL with TMZ (as compared to chemotherapy alone). Altogether, MSCs induced PN-to-MES transition can strongly contribute to therapy resistance and tumor relapse. Systemic administration of Galunisertib blocks this pathological pathway and supports standard clinical care.

title: Identification of a Kinase-Autophagy Signaling Hub as a Therapeutic Vulnerability in Pediatric Glioma

affiliations.name: Koç University
Sabancı University
University of Fribourg

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric glioma remains a devastating malignancy characterized by a profound lack of effective therapeutic interventions. This study identifies a specific stress-responsive kinase as a pivotal regulator of autophagy in pediatric glioma cells. Autophagy is a cellular recycling process essential for maintaining homeostasis and ensuring tumor survival under nutrient, energy, and amino acid deprivation. Through SILAC-MS/MS, co-immunoprecipitation, and colocalization analyses, we demonstrated that this kinase directly interacts with the key autophagy proteins, an association that is significantly enriched during autophagy-inducing stress. Functional validation reveals that the kinase is essential for pathway activation, as its knockout significantly impairs autophagy, whereas its overexpression is sufficient to initiate the process under basal conditions and amplify it under stress. Furthermore, our proteomics-based mapping of the kinase interactome and its phosphorylation targets uncovered several novel partners. By establishing this kinase as a central modulator of autophagic flux, our findings provide critical insights into basic cellular mechanisms and highlight the targeting of this kinase-autophagy axis as a promising therapeutic strategy for the treatment of pediatric glioma.

title: IL-12-Armed EGFRvIII-Retargeted Oncolytic HSV Promotes Agnostic Vaccination in Heterogeneous Murine Glioblastoma

affiliations.name: AOM Ospedale Policlinico San Martino
University of Genoa
Università di Bologna

bodyParagraphs: Tumor heterogeneity represents one of the major obstacles to targeted glioblastoma therapies, since any treatment directed against a specific molecular target may spare tumor cell populations lacking its expression. We hypothesized that this limitation could be overcome by using a retargeted oncolytic HSV (ReHV) to deliver IL-12 selectively within the tumor. While viral infection and oncolysis remain restricted to target-positive cells, local IL-12-mediated immune stimulation is expected to induce an agnostic vaccination, extending the antitumor response to cells that cannot be directly infected by the virus.

We tested an EGFRvIII-retargeted ReHV expressing murine IL-12 in immunocompetent mice orthotopically transplanted with glioblastoma cells. Two independent models entirely composed of EGFRvIII-positive cells were analyzed together with a heterogeneous model containing both EGFRvIII-positive and EGFRvIII-negative cells. Animals were treated seven days after transplantation and tumor progression was monitored weekly by MRI.

In both homogeneous models, treatment consistently delayed tumor growth and substantially prolonged survival, increasing median survival by approximately 1.5-to 2-fold compared with untreated controls, with complete tumor eradication observed in a subset of animals. Importantly, therapeutic efficacy was also maintained in heterogeneous tumors, despite the presence of cells lacking the viral target. In this setting, median survival more than doubled, and almost half of the treated animals showed long-term survival without detectable tumor. MRI analysis confirmed a marked delay in tumor growth following treatment. Preliminary rechallenge experiments in long-surviving mice also showed protection against subsequent tumor transplantation.

These findings support the ability of IL-12-armed ReHV to convert selective viral targeting into a broader immune-mediated response, providing experimental evidence for an agnostic vaccination strategy capable of overcoming glioblastoma heterogeneity.

title: Influence of astrocyte-glioblastoma cell interactions on proliferation and migration

affiliations.name: Department of Anatomy and Cell Biology
Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive tumor that proliferates and invades the brain tissue through complex interaction with the surrounding microenvironment. Of particular importance are the interactions between tumor cells and glial cells, amongst others astrocytes, which contribute to the modulation of tumor behavior. This study compares the pro-tumorous features of two GBM cell lines (LN229 and U138) and astrocytes under monoculture and co-culture conditions. Since, inflammation is associated with tumor progression, the role of the pro-inflammatory activated astrocytes on proliferation and 3D spheroid generation was assessed. Primary murine astrocytes and the murine astrocytic cell line C8-D1A were used under control condition, and in a pro-inflammatory A1-activated state. First, the cell-cell interactions were analyzed in 2D co-culture model. To characterize further cell-cell interactions, 3D co-cultures were established to mimic the tumor growth in a more complex microenvironment. Proliferation and cell cycle dynamics were characterized using FACS analysis and immunohistochemical staining (Ki67, BrdU), while molecules involved in cytoskeletal reorganization and cell-cell contacts in GBM cells were investigated by qRT-PCR and Western blot. 2D live cell-imaging revealed high migratory and proliferative profile of GBM cells, meanwhile human astrocytes exhibited a stable non-proliferative profile. Co-culture with astrocytes, significantly slowed down movement of the GBM cell lines. Analysis of cytoskeleton-associated mRNA in GBM cells demonstrated amongst others, elevation of RhoA and β-Catenin expression. In 3D co-culture systems, an initial acceleration of aggregation dynamics was present in both GBM cell lines. After 72 h of GBM-astrocyte co-cultures showed a reduced BrdU incorporation and an accumulation of cells in the G0/G1 phase, despite increased Ki67 expression. Overall, these findings suggest that astrocytes mitigate cell growth and motility of the GBM cells contributing to the confinement of tumor spreading. Furthermore, pro-inflammatory activation of astrocytes seems to influence the proliferation and reduce growth behavior of GBM cells.

title: Integrated Spatial Profiling Identifies a Recruitment-Deficient Lymphocyte-Cold State in Meningioma

programme.programmeTitle: Integrated Spatial Profiling Identifies a Recruitment-Deficient Lymphocyte-Cold State in Meningioma
programme.sessionTitle: Pediatric, Low-grade and Rare CNS Tumors

affiliations.name: Klinik für Neurochirurgie,Universitätsklinikum Freiburg
Medizinische Fakultät
Institut of Neuropathologie, Universitätsklinikum Heidelberg
Klinik für Neurochirurgie, Universitätsklinikum Dresden

bodyParagraphs: Background: Immune checkpoint blockade has shown limited efficacy in meningioma, yet the mechanisms underlying immune resistance remain unclear. While hypoxic, macrophage-rich niches have been implicated in immune evasion, it remains unresolved whether lymphocyte-cold tumors result from local T-cell exclusion, T-cell dysfunction, or defective immune recruitment. We integrated transcriptomic, spatial, and protein-level profiling to define the meningioma immune microenvironment and established a patient-derived slice-culture platform for functional validation.

Methods: Bulk RNA-seq from 273 meningiomas was integrated with multiplex immunofluorescence (42 WHO grade I–II tumors), spatial transcriptomics (29 Visium sections), and single-nucleus RNA-seq (26 tumors; 44,266 cells). Spatial autocorrelation and neighborhood enrichment analyses quantified relationships between T cells, hypoxia, and macrophage-rich niches. Patient-derived organotypic slice cultures co-cultured with matched autologous PBMCs or isolated CD8 T cells were established for mechanistic studies using live-cell imaging, multiplex immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, and CXCL9/CXCL10 ELISA.

Results: Bulk transcriptomics identified reproducible immune microenvironment states independent of tumor grade and associated with coordinated hypoxic, angiogenic, and macrophage-related programs. Multiplex immunofluorescence confirmed organized CA9⁺/SPP1⁺/CD163⁺ macrophage-rich niches. Despite prominent macrophage clustering, CD3⁺ T cells remained diffusely distributed and were not depleted from hypoxic macrophage-rich regions, arguing against local macrophage-mediated exclusion as the mechanism underlying the lymphocyte-cold phenotype. Across bulk, spatial, and single-nucleus datasets, lymphocyte-cold tumors demonstrated impaired T-cell recruitment programs, characterized by reduced CXCL9–CXCR3 signaling despite preserved myeloid infiltration. Patient-derived slice cultures with matched autologous immune cells enabled assessment of T-cell recruitment into intact tumor tissue and provide a platform to perturb the CXCL9/CXCR3 axis.

Conclusions: Integrated spatial profiling identifies lymphocyte-cold meningiomas as a recruitment-deficient immune state rather than one driven by local T-cell exclusion. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for the limited efficacy of checkpoint blockade and nominate restoration of CXCL9–CXCR3-mediated T-cell recruitment as a therapeutic strategy.

title: Intraclonal diversification and cell competition shape evolutionary trajectories in glioblastoma

affiliations.name: University of Genoa
IRCCS AOM San Martino Hospital

bodyParagraphs: Tumor evolution is widely recognized as a major driver of resistance, but it may also represent a novel therapeutic opportunity if its underlying rules can be deciphered and hijacked. We previously showed that glioblastoma progression is characterized by extensive clonal extinction driven by cell competition, a process that continues within established clones and progressively reshapes their composition. Here, we investigated how phenotypic diversity arises from the progeny of a single glioma cell. Cells derived from monoclonal murine gliomas were labeled with transcribed genetic barcodes and profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing at baseline. Subclonal dynamics were then followed by longitudinal barcode sequencing across multiple independent expansion experiments, allowing direct reconstruction of evolutionary trajectories and their relationship with transcriptional states. Although all cells originated from a single founder, subclones diversified into distinct phenotypic states. Across independent evolution experiments, we observed the emergence of stable high-fitness populations, the replacement between competing states, and transient populations that expanded before progressively disappearing. These patterns were highly consistent across experiments, suggesting that cell-intrinsic determinants commit subclones toward reproducible long-term evolutionary trajectories. Transcriptional profiling identified gene programs associated with the current fitness of individual subclones, but did not predict their future evolutionary behavior, despite the predetermination we observed. These findings suggest even if the determinants of future fitness are already established within tumor populations, they are not reflected in their transcriptional state. Our results indicate that glioblastoma evolution is shaped by the continuous generation of phenotypic diversity followed by reproducible fitness-based selection. Rather than representing a purely stochastic process, tumor evolution appears to follow exploitable biological constraints. Defining the mechanisms underlying these hidden fitness states may provide a framework to manipulate clonal competition and direct tumor evolution toward more therapeutically vulnerable conditions.
body: Tumor evolution is widely recognized as a major driver of resistance, but it may also represent a novel therapeutic opportunity if its underlying rules can be deciphered and hijacked. We previously showed that glioblastoma progression is characterized by extensive clonal extinction driven by cell competition, a process that continues within established clones and progressively reshapes their composition. Here, we investigated how phenotypic diversity arises from the progeny of a single glioma cell. Cells derived from monoclonal murine gliomas were labeled with transcribed genetic barcodes and profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing at baseline. Subclonal dynamics were then followed by longitudinal barcode sequencing across multiple independent expansion experiments, allowing direct reconstruction of evolutionary trajectories and their relationship with transcriptional states. Although all cells originated from a single founder, subclones diversified into distinct phenotypic states. Across independent evolution experiments, we observed the emergence of stable high-fitness populations, the replacement between competing states, and transient populations that expanded before progressively disappearing. These patterns were highly consistent across experiments, suggesting that cell-intrinsic determinants commit subclones toward reproducible long-term evolutionary trajectories. Transcriptional profiling identified gene programs associated with the current fitness of individual subclones, but did not predict their future evolutionary behavior, despite the predetermination we observed. These findings suggest even if the determinants of future fitness are already established within tumor populations, they are not reflected in their transcriptional state. Our results indicate that glioblastoma evolution is shaped by the continuous generation of phenotypic diversity followed by reproducible fitness-based selection. Rather than representing a purely stochastic process, tumor evolution appears to follow exploitable biological constraints. Defining the mechanisms underlying these hidden fitness states may provide a framework to manipulate clonal competition and direct tumor evolution toward more therapeutically vulnerable conditions.

title: Investigating Synergistic Temozolomide Based Combinations with Rifampicin, Ulipristal, and EdU in U87 Glioblastoma Cells

affiliations.name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Graduate School of Health Sciences,Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Istanbul, Türkiye
Department of Medical Biochemistry, School of Medicine, Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Istanbul, Türkiye

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults and remains associated with poor survival despite current standard therapy. The clinical efficacy of temozolomide (TMZ), the standard chemotherapeutic agent for GBM, is limited by intrinsic and acquired resistance mechanisms, including enhanced DNA damage repair. Drug repurposing based combination strategies may improve treatment response by simultaneously targeting complementary resistance-associated pathways. This study aimed to evaluate the in vitro cytotoxic efficacy and synergistic potential of TMZ combined with three repurposed agents targeting distinct pathways: rifampicin (an RNA polymerase inhibitor), ulipristal (a progesterone receptor antagonist), and 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU; a DNA damage enhancer), using the U87 human glioblastoma cell line.

IC50 values were determined by MTT cell viability assays following dose-response experiments performed within the following concentration ranges: TMZ (100 µM–1 mM), EdU (1–50 µM), ulipristal (100 µM–1 mM), and rifampicin (50–250 µM). Based on monotherapy IC50 values, eight treatment groups were established: control, TMZ, TMZ+EdU, TMZ+rifampicin, TMZ+ulipristal, TMZ+EdU+rifampicin, TMZ+EdU+ulipristal, and TMZ+EdU+ulipristal+rifampicin. Drug interactions were quantified by Combination Index (CI) analysis using the Chou–Talalay method implemented in CompuSyn.

Monotherapy assays enabled determination of IC50 values for each agent. In combination analyses, multiple TMZ based regimens showed synergistic cytotoxicity (CI < 1) and greater anti-proliferative effects than single-agent treatment in U87 cells. These findings establish an in vitro basis for subsequent analyses of real-time cytotoxicity kinetics, apoptosis induction, cell invasion, and resistance-associated metabolic alterations by untargeted LC-MS/MS metabolomics. Overall, the results support the potential of TMZ based multi-drug combinations as a preclinical strategy for targeting resistance associated pathways in glioblastoma.
Keywords: Glioblastoma, Temozolomide, EdU, Ulipristal, Rifampicin, Combinational therapy.

title: LC-MS/MS-Based Metabolomic Analysis of ATRA and Curcumin Combination Treatment in U87-MG Glioblastoma Cells

affiliations.name: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Graduate School of Health Sciences,Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Istanbul, Türkiye
Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Faculty of Engineering and Natural Sciences, Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Istanbul, Türkiye
Department of Medical Biochemistry, School of Medicine, Acıbadem Mehmet Ali Aydınlar University, Istanbul, Türkiye

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor characterized by metabolic plasticity and resistance to conventional therapies. Understanding treatment-induced metabolic alterations may provide insight into mechanisms of therapeutic response and potential metabolic vulnerabilities in GBM. This study aimed to characterize metabolic alterations induced by all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), curcumin (CURC), and their combination in U87-MG glioblastoma cells using LC-MS/MS-based untargeted metabolomics. U87-MG cells were treated with ATRA (75 µM), CURC (20 µM), or their combination for 72 h. Intracellular metabolites were analyzed using UHPLC coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 240 high resolution mass spectrometer. Data processing and metabolite annotation were performed using Compound Discoverer 3.3. Significantly altered metabolites (p<0.05 and |log₂FC|>1) were subjected to pathway enrichment analysis using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 and KEGG. Metabolomic profiling identified 46, 77, and 74 significantly altered metabolites following ATRA, CURC, and combination treatment, respectively. ATRA affected sphingolipid, tryptophan, and glutathione metabolism, whereas CURC predominantly altered methionine and purine metabolism. Combination treatment induced broader metabolic changes involving spermidine biosynthesis, methionine and purine metabolism, glutathione metabolism, pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis, betaine metabolism, thiamine metabolism, and sphingolipid metabolism. ATRA and CURC induced distinct metabolic responses in glioblastoma cells, while their combination was associated with broader metabolic reprogramming involving amino acid, nucleotide, lipid, polyamine, and redox-related pathways. These findings provide insight into treatment-associated metabolic adaptations in GBM cells and the molecular mechanisms underlying the response of glioblastoma cells to combined ATRA and CURC treatment. Further studies integrating metabolomic findings with functional validation and additional molecular approaches are necessary to clarify the biological significance of these metabolic alterations and their potential relevance to future therapeutic strategies for GBM.
Keywords: Glioblastoma; ATRA; Curcumin; Untargeted Metabolomics; LC-MS/MS; Metabolic Reprogramming.

title: Liquid Biopsy-Based Methylation and Fragment Signatures in Intracranial Meningiomas

affiliations.name: Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, Neuroscience Institute
Lithuanian University of Health Sciences

bodyParagraphs: Intracranial meningiomas are the most common primary tumors of the central nervous system. Although the majority are histologically benign, their biological behavior is highly heterogeneous, with some tumors demonstrating aggressive growth, recurrence, or resistance to treatment. Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery (GKRS) is widely used for the management of selected meningiomas. However, predicting individual treatment response remains challenging because reliable non-invasive molecular biomarkers are lacking. Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) represents a promising source of tumor-derived molecular information, with both DNA methylation patterns and fragment profiles reflecting disease-specific biological processes. This study aims to characterize plasma cfDNA methylation and nucleosome fragment populations in patients with intracranial meningiomas and healthy individuals to identify biomarkers associated with tumor presence and response to GKRS. The study cohort comprised 53 patients with intracranial meningiomas who underwent blood sampling immediately before GKRS and at a six-month follow-up, together with 20 age-matched healthy controls. Plasma cfDNA was isolated using the QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit and quantified using the Qubit fluorometric assay. Fragment size distribution was assessed using the Agilent TapeStation system, enabling characterization of mono-, di-, and tri-nucleosome cfDNA populations. Genome-wide profiling of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) was performed using Oxford Nanopore sequencing. Fragment profiles and methylation signatures were compared between patients and controls and evaluated in relation to clinical characteristics. The ongoing study identified distinct methylation and fragment signatures associated with meningioma profiling and patient response to GKRS.

title: Liquid Crystal-like Self-Organization of Glioblastoma is Associated with Consistent Cell Migration

affiliations.name: Department of Anatomy and Cell Biology, Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg
Department of Neurosurgery, Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma is the most lethal and frequent type of primary brain tumors, characterized by a high proliferative and infiltrative capacity. Here, we used live cell imaging to analyze the effect of cell density variations on the migratory capacity of established and primary glioblastoma cell lines. We found that proliferation events promoted local velocity of glioblastoma cells, up to three cell-length away from the proliferation event. Furthermore, two phenotypes were found when subjecting glioblastoma cells to a cell density gradient. While one phenotype was characterized by the active migration of cells, independent of proliferation, the other was mostly driven by cell proliferation. Lastly, the analysis of effects of an overall increasing cell density demonstrated that cells showing signs of self-organization, forming liquid crystal-like structures are able to maintain a high migratory potential even for high cell densities, normally considered to result in a migratory arrest. Notably, the emergence of small-scale liquid crystal-like order was associated with a better maintenance of cellular migration, even in cell populations that were otherwise largely in a state of migratory arrest. Thus, structure formation might help glioblastoma cells to move efficiently in states of high confinement, maintaining infiltrative properties.

title: Local calvarial myeloid reservoirs do not contribute to tumor associated macrophages in Glioblastoma

affiliations.name: University Hospital, LMU Munich, Munich, Germany

bodyParagraphs: Recent evidence shows that monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) invading into the brain can have a dual source: the adjacent skull bone marrow via direct dural vascular channels and the systemic blood circulation. The MDMs can seed the brain parenchyma under acute neuroinflammation and infiltrate the microglia-free brain. Although monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) represent a major subset of tumor-associated macrophages in glioblastoma (GBM), local calvarial marrow is increasingly recognized as an active source of immune cells during CNS malignancy, supplying cells of the adaptive immune system or neutrophils to the tumor. Whether skull-derived macrophages are also actively recruited to the GBM microenvironment, however, remains unclear. To track the specific contribution of skull bone marrow-derived macrophages during tumor growth, we performed calvarial skull flap transplantation from Cx3cr1-GFP donor mice into Cx3cr1::CreERT2;PU.1fl/fl recipient mice. Conditional PU.1 knockout in microglia and macrophages cells induced a strong (95%) and long-lasting reduction in CNS myeloid cell populations. Into the same model we orthotopically implanted GBM cells. We analysed the mouse brains using confocal microscopy to visualize and quantify donor skull-derived Cx3cr1-GFP cell infiltration. Surprisingly, we didn’t observe skull bone marrow-derived MDMs in GBM. This lack of engraftment was consistent across all examined areas. These findings indicate that the MDMs recruited to glioblastoma arise dominantly from the systemic blood circulation, rather than from the adjacent skull marrow. This finding suggests a distinct tumor-driven recruitment program that bypasses the local calvarial bone marrow.

title: Local strategy to remodel the glioblastoma microenvironment and “open the door” to anti-tumoral immune cells

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GB) is a highly aggressive brain tumor associated with extremely poor prognosis. The failure of current curative strategies is driven by a marked hypoxic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment along with recurrence. Our objective is to develop a novel therapeutic approach based on a hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogel engrafted with a selective chemokine designed to stimulate anti-tumor immune responses and contribute to cognitive recovery following tumor resection. First, through gene signatures analyses from TCGA bulk RNA-seq database, we identified absence of markers of early, immature and mature tertiary lymphoid organs (TLOs) in GB including some chemokines involved in the establishment of mature TLO structures. We here investigated the therapeutic potential of a selective chemokine delivered within the cavity resection through our thermosensitive HA-hydrogel. Following murine GB resection in immunocompetent mice, the HA-based hydrogel containing a free chemokine significantly reduced tumor recurrence volume, promoted MECA79+ high endothelial venule (HEV)-like immature structures and increased immune cell infiltration notably CD20+ B-cell recruitment. while improving mouse survival. This response was associated with the formation of B-cell aggregates in the pericavity tissue and infiltration of B cells into the dura mater characterized thanks to an original whole-head imaging protocol combined with a 3D bone-clearing approach preserving the skull bone. This currently allows evaluation of our strategy on vascular architecture remodeling and TLOs formation. Finally, to test the resection cavity refunctionalization, we led longitudinal behavioral analyses comparing GB, resection+HA and resection+HA+chemokine mice and showed that chemokine restored anxiety-related behavior and improved cognitive performance, both altered by the tumor. Together, these findings demonstrate that local delivery of a key chemokine through a thermosensitive HA-hydrogel is a promising therapeutic strategy against glioblastoma. Supported by Ligue contre le Cancer Normandie, Région Normandie et les Fonds Européens du Développement Régional (FEDER), Géfluc, Université de Rouen Normandie and Inserm.

This response was associated with the formation of B-cell aggregates in the pericavity tissue and infiltration of B cells into the dura mater characterized thanks to an original whole-head imaging protocol combined with a 3D bone-clearing approach preserving the skull bone. This currently allows evaluation of our strategy on vascular architecture remodeling and TLOs formation. Finally, to test the resection cavity refunctionalization, we led longitudinal behavioral analyses comparing GB, resection+HA and resection+HA+chemokine mice and showed that chemokine restored anxiety-related behavior and improved cognitive performance, both altered by the tumor. Together, these findings demonstrate that local delivery of a key chemokine through a thermosensitive HA-hydrogel is a promising therapeutic strategy against glioblastoma. bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Low-grade gliomas (LGG) represent the most common type of solid brain tumor diagnosed in children and young adults in Germany. Since 2019, all confirmed cases have been centrally documented in a national registry. This registry supports the investigation of clinical and scientific questions by a multidisciplinary team. The present study aims to gain deeper insight into neurosurgical treatment patterns employed in infants diagnosed with low-grade glioma in Germany since the establishment of the registry. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study is based on data collected by the national HIT-LOGGIC registry from 2019 to 2025. Infants aged 0 to 24 months at diagnosis with LGG were included. Collected data encompassed demographics, clinical characteristics, surgical interventions, neuropathological findings, and non-surgical treatments. The primary aim was to analyze neurosurgical management strategies within this cohort. Results: A total of 174 patients were identified, with a median (Q1-Q3) age at diagnosis of 11.9 (5.6-

18.8) months. Optic pathway was the most prominent localization, accounting for 47.7% of cases. The rate of primary tumor dissemination in this cohort was 15.4%. Pilocytic astrocytoma was diagnosed in 61% of cases. Surgical therapy alone achieved disease control in 29.9% of cases and was most frequently sufficient for hemispheric low-grade gliomas (75%) and cerebellar low-grade gliomas (68.4%). 53.4% of patients required additional systemic therapy. The overall neurosurgical adverse event rate considering all tumor resections or biopsies performed, was 28.1% (N=48/171) with clinical neurological events occurring in 18.1% (N=31/171) and surgery related complications in 14% (N=24/171), while 54.2% (N=26/48) were transient. Conclusions: Infants with LGG represent a more challenging cohort of patients for the multidisciplinary team. Surgical treatment remains the most relevant initial therapy. While patient age alone does not significantly influence surgical decision-making, tumor location plays a critical role in determining the therapeutic efficiency.

bodyParagraphs: Background: While pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG) generally exhibit favorable 10-year overall survival (OS) rates, infants comprise a high-risk cohort with increased morbidity and mortality. Utilizing molecular and clinical data from the prospective German HIT-LOGGIC registry, this study aims to detect additional prognostic risk factors within this specific patient population. Methods: We extracted clinical, neuroradiological, histopathological, and molecular profiles from the HIT-LOGGIC registry and the LOGGIC Core Bioclinical Data Bank. Patients under two years of age with a radiologically or histologically confirmed diagnosis of pLGGs were included. Results: In Germany, infant pLGG demonstrated an annual incidence ranging from 1.4 to 2.6 cases per 100,000 infants. Within our cohort of 177 patients, diagnosis within the first six months of life, presence of diencephalic syndrome, larger absolute tumor volume, and leptomeningeal dissemination emerged as significant independent predictors of reduced overall and progression-free survival. A markedly higher frequency of tumors had no identifiable molecular driver compared to the broader pLGG population (24% vs. 3%), alongside an enriched prevalence of BRAF V600E alterations (21% vs. 10%). Notably, the molecular profile of the eleven deceased patients did not differ compared from that of the general cohort. Conclusions: Infants diagnosed with pLGG under six months of age experience a worse prognosis regarding survival and long-term morbidity; however, definitive molecular drivers remain elusive. Broadening the scope of advanced molecular diagnostics and investigating the role of the tumor microenvironment are critical steps for future risk stratification.

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric diffuse gliomas are a group of devastating childhood brain cancers that span diverse histomolecular subtypes. Gliomatosis cerebri (GC) represents a radiologically defined, highly invasive growth pattern that can occur across distinct glioma subtypes. The molecular and cellular basis of the GC phenotype remains largely elusive, partly because limited clinical annotation has constrained access to tumor material for systematic investigation. To address this, we established a multinational GC consortium assembling tumor specimens from 21 primary pediatric GC patients across the US and Europe (1–18 years). We developed an integrated multi-center framework combining clinical, radiologic, histomolecular, and multiomic tumor profiling, including single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; Smart-seq2), spatial transcriptomics (10x Xenium), and spatial proteomics (imaging mass cytometry), with complementary patient-derived functional modeling. Consistent with previous reports, pediatric GC predominantly arises in H3/IDH-wildtype pediatric high-grade glioma (pedHGG; 17/21), particularly the methylation-defined subclass pedHGG_RTK2A (7/21). Genomic profiling reveals recurrent alterations in EGFR (7/21), PIK3CA/PIK3R1 (7/21 combined), TERT (7/21), and BCOR (6/21). Our snRNA-seq analyses reveal marked inter-and intratumoral heterogeneity, with recurrent AC-like, OPC-like, NPC-like, and MES-like malignant cell states identified across the cohort, suggesting an interplay of multiple cellular programs underlying GC invasion. Building on these findings, our integrated spatial multiomic analyses define the in situ organization of cell populations and assess invasion-permissive cellular niches. Complementary patient-derived tumor–neuronal co-culture and xenograft models further interrogate how tumor-intrinsic cellular programs and microenvironmental interactions cooperate to drive brain-wide dissemination in pediatric GC. Together, this work establishes the first comprehensive, high-resolution atlas of pediatric GC and provides an integrated view of the molecular, cellular, and spatial features associated with diffuse brain invasion. These insights may enable more precise biological classification and inform new avenues for therapeutic intervention in this dismal pediatric disease.

bodyParagraphs: Background: Modulation of lipid metabolism through myelin recycling has recently emerged as a critical driver of macrophage-mediated immunosuppression and tumor progression in glioblastoma. However, the underlying mechanisms in brain metastases remain poorly characterized. Methods: We aimed to reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in experimental brain metastasis models by combining radiotherapy with either adenosine signalling blockade or immune checkpoint inhibition. Comprehensive immunophenotyping including multiplexed histology, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and metabolomics was performed to delineate immunomodulatory effects. Macrophages in ex vivo Cancer Core Models, consisting brain metastatic tissue embedded in cerebral organoids, were stimulated with myelin to induce lipid-laden macrophage (LLM) and assess functional consequences for cancer cell proliferation, macrophage activation, and T cell responses using imaging and transcriptomic profiling. Macrophages were further modulated by supplementing adenosine or inosine, as well as by neutralizing antibodies targeting cell–cell communication between LLMs and T cells. Results: In mouse breast-to-brain metastasis, radiotherapy induced a pronounced expansion of lipid-laden macrophages characterized by immunosuppressive polarization, reduced antigen presentation, and impaired T cell activation. Cell–cell interaction analyses revealed macrophage-mediated FN1 and SPP1 suppressive signaling to limit T cell responses and therapeutic efficacy. In contrast, combining radiotherapy with adenosine signaling blockade prevented LLM accumulation and promoted expansion of antigen-presenting macrophages, resulting in significant survival benefits. Ex vivo models recapitulated the induction of LLMs and confirmed their immunosuppressive function. Notably, macrophage modulation exhibited heterogeneity across different brain metastatic origins, including lung cancer and melanoma. Metabolomic profiling of breast-to-brain metastasis treated with radiotherapy and/or immunotherapy revealed distinct alterations in metabolites and lipid species critical for macrophage function, including adenosine, sphingomyelin, ceramide, and phosphatidylcholine. Conclusion: Targeted modulation of lipid metabolism in tumor-associated macrophages represents a promising therapeutic strategy to alleviate immunosuppression and enhance anti-tumor immunity in brain metastases.

bodyParagraphs: The cellular composition and interactions within the glioblastoma (GBM) microenvironment evolve and influence pathology. However, tumor-parenchymal interactions at early stages of tumorigenesis or GBM relapse remain insufficiently characterized. To explore the vascular microenvironment during initiation, compared to tumor-free controls, we developed a methodology in orthotopic GBM mouse models tracing endothelia, mural cells, and neighboring cell types. Lineage analysis in vascular cells was achieved with transgenic strains containing fluorescent reporters. Transfer of fluorescently-labeled, capillary-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) identified vessel-associated cells in GBM. Dual-fluorescent transgenic GBM models tracking endothelial cells and tumor-associated macrophages displayed EV-transfer over a narrow spatial margin in CNS neoplasms, but not under physiological conditions. Endothelial-derived EV-uptake in other parenchymal populations was observed with immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy. ImageStream-flow-cytometry corroborated this, and traced vascular or EV-labeled vessel-neighboring cells were sorted for single-cell transcriptomics (scRNAseq) at 4 and 14 days. Under physiological conditions, scRNAseq showed that our transgenic lineage-tracing models specifically indicate vascular cells plus smaller macrophage and astrocyte fractions. In GBM tracing models, vessel-associated myeloid cells are increased in the tumor-free hemisphere, with a surge in vessel-associated cells in GBM. Thus, tumor-initiated EV-transfer identified the vascular microenvironment in early and advanced GBM. Strikingly, scRNAseq indicated neural crest-like cells (NCC-like cells), recently discovered in human GBM, within the GBM vascular microenvironment. NCC-like cells are part of the brain injury response to surgical lesions. To determine if NCC-like cells resulted from tumor implantation or initiation, we investigated a transgenic GBM model discriminating these aspects. This model showed that NCC-like cells accumulate in GBM spontaneously. We demonstrated that endothelial-derived vesicle uptake can identify cells associated with the vascular tumor microenvironment even in small tumors. The identification of an early-enriched NCC-like population highlights an underappreciated component of the developing GBM microenvironment and provides a basis to investigate its role in initiation and relapse.

bodyParagraphs: Context: Glioblastoma (GB) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, with no curative treatment. During perivascular invasion, GB cells migrate through constrained environments under astrocytic endfeet in response to growth factors. We investigated how mechanical stress influences nuclear envelope (NE) integrity, molecular heterogeneity and GB aggressiveness. Methods and results: Adherent and patient-derived GB cell lines were not exposed or exposed to an EGF gradient to induce migration in transwell with or without physical constraints (cGB and ncGB). Without EGF, mechanical stress reduced the NE proteins Emerin and SUN1, decreased nuclear circularity, increased micronuclei formation, and H3K9me3 and γ-H2AX foci, suggesting epigenetic and genetic alterations. In contrast, EGF increased lamin A/C expression, preserved nuclear shape, and limited membrane rupture and micronuclei formation under constraint. Using time-lapse videomicroscopy in a PDMS microfluidic device with 3 µm constrictions, we observed sequential NE bleb formation and lamin A/C “scar” formation, suggesting a dynamic repair network maintaining NE integrity. Proteomic studies of nuclear contents reveal that pathways associated with transcription and spliceosome, metabolic processes and chemokine signaling while RNA-seq confirmed acquired migratory, mesenchymal and immune-related transcriptional programs, specific of confined GB cells. Indeed, these cells exhibited increased proliferation, invasion and resistance to temozolomide. In vivo, immunodeficient mice xenografted with cGB-U87-eGFP+EGF cells showed a 12% decrease in median survival compared with respective ncGB controls. cGB+EGF tumors show increased size and cell density, higher lamin A/C in both tumor core and perivascular infiltrating cells, increased F4/80+

macrophages and reduced Iba1+/CD68+ activated microglia within the bulk GB. Conclusion: We highlight an original and complex link between physical stress, the expression of NE structural proteins and the protecting role of EGF on the NE integrity during migration under constraint leading to a transition towards and immunosuppressor phenotype and exacerbated aggressiveness likely accompanying recurrence.

title: Phenotypic Screening Identifies Flunarizine as an Inhibitor of Radiotherapy-Induced Astrocyte Reactivity with Therapeutic Potential in Glioblastoma

programme.programmeTitle: Phenotypic Screening Identifies Flunarizine as an Inhibitor of Radiotherapy-Induced Astrocyte Reactivity with Therapeutic Potential in Glioblastoma

affiliations.name: Lund University

bodyParagraphs: Radiotherapy is part of the standard-of-care for glioblastoma, yet tumors invariably recur as incurable lesions post-treatment. Recent studies suggest that radiation-induced astrocyte reactivity fosters a tumor-supportive environment, however effective strategies targeting reactive astrocyte phenotypes are lacking. Using a novel image-based assay, we screened over 1,700 small molecule compounds, identifying 29 that inhibit radiation-induced astrocyte reactivity in human astrocytes. Among these, Flunarizine, a calcium-entry blocker approved for migraine treatment, significantly reduced astrocyte reactivity in vitro and in vivo. In a genetically engineered glioblastoma mouse model, combining Flunarizine with radiotherapy markedly improved survival without affecting unirradiated controls, indicating specificity for a radiation-induced phenotype. Mechanistically, Flunarizine inhibited radiation-induced fibrosis in vivo and directly suppressed astrocytic TGF-beta activation in vitro. Notably, Flunarizine treatment had no direct effect on primary glioblastoma cells, emphasizing its microenvironmental specificity. In conclusion, we identified Flunarizine as a promising repurposed compound capable of effectively mitigating radiation-induced astrocyte reactivity and delaying glioblastoma recurrence. This approach offers a viable therapeutic strategy to enhance current glioblastoma treatments.

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric-type diffuse high-grade gliomas (pHGGs) are aggressive central nervous system tumors that are the leading cause of cancer-related death in children. pHGGs comprise histologically, genetically, and molecularly distinct subtypes with characteristic driver mutations, anatomical localizations, and ages of onset. Although pHGGs share many features with adult gliomas, they represent clinically and biologically distinct tumor entities. Despite growing insights into the cellular architectures of pHGGs, the evolution of malignant cell states and tumor microenvironments during tumor progression remains largely unexplored. In this study, we generated an extensive longitudinal single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic atlas of pediatric high-grade gliomas (pHGG) from children, adolescents and young adults using single-nucleus RNA sequencing and Xenium In Situ spatial transcriptomics. Our cohort includes 49 paired HGG samples across tumor subtypes, spanning diffuse midline glioma (DMG), IDH-mutant (IDH-HGG) and H3-and IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma (HGG), representing the most comprehensive longitudinal pediatric glioma cohort profiled to date. Single-nucleus profiling uncovered shared and distinct cellular subpopulations in different pHGG subtypes. Despite notable similarities in transcriptional profiles of primary and recurrent pHGGs, recurrent HGGs showed increased proportions of malignant cells with a hypoxia-associated program, coupled with a reduction in malignant glial-like cell populations. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of 71 tumor sections from 31 pHGGs revealed subtype-specific global spatial organizations and localized cellular niches. Upon analyzing the density of tissue regions, we found that the normal cells occur in less dense regions than malignant cells; within the malignant compartments, we found OPC-like cells consistently existed in denser regions than AC-like cells. Overall, our study characterizes the cellular landscape and spatial architecture across pHGG subtypes and provides a detailed delineation of the spatiotemporal dynamics during progression, paving the way for the identification of novel therapeutic targets.

bodyParagraphs: Molecular pathology in routine diagnostic workup of pediatric low grade glioma (pLGG) tissue currently redefines the disease. Genetic workup of pLGG tumor tissue within the LOGGIC and LOGGIC Core registries includes an epigenetic profiling, NGS sequencing of 201 brain tumor-relevant genes and RNA sequencing. This offers to detect driver alterations in 97% of pLGG and therefor sets the stage for personalized medicine for the majority of pLGG patients. KIAA1549::BRAF fusions compose 50-60% of detected alterations, while rare fusions including FGFR1 fusions compose with 10-20% the second largest group of genetic alterations.

Rare fusions beyond KIAA1549::BRAF to date have not yet been systematically described in pLGG glioma. Our aim is to offer clinicians of patients with rare fusions a reference on what to expect regarding clinical behavior of the tumor and treatment efficacies. Of 2700 patients registered in the HIT-LOGGIC registry between April 2019 and March 2025, 1028 were also registered in the LOGGIC Core bioclinical databank. 548 tumors received mRNA sequencing. Via mRNA sequencing 97 patients with tumors bearing non-KIAA1549::BRAF, non-FGFR fusions were identified as rare-fusion cohort. The most common fusion partners involved were BRAF (29), MYB(L) (16), RAF1 (13), NTRK 1-3 fusions (15), MYB::QKI (8), and GOPC::ROS (5). Rare gene fusions with specific fusion partners correlated with defined histologic entities of pLGG. Rare BRAF fusions mainly occurred in pilocytic astrocytoma, while MYB::QKI fusions

occurred in angiocentric glioma or MYB/MYBL1-altered diffuse astrocytoma. BRAF breakpoints of rare BRAF fusions were mostly equivalent to canonical BRAF breakpoints described for KIAA1549::BRAF. However the frequency distribution differed significantly, with rare breakpoints in the context of KIAA1549::BRAF being the most common breakpoints among rare BRAF fusions.

Here, we systematically describe rare fusions in pLGG identified via mRNA sequencing and link molecular pathology to clinical features and patient courses, including sensitivity to different therapeutic regimen.

title: RAD52 Proteomic Analysis in Glioblastoma Cell Hierarchy

affiliations.name: Institute of Biomedicine of Seville, IBiS/Virgen del Rocío University Hospital/CSIC/University of Seville, Spain

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive primary brain tumour in adults and is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and inevitable recurrence following standard therapy. This recurrence is driven by Glioblastoma Stem-like Cells (GSCs), a subpopulation with high self-renewal capacity, enhanced DNA repair activity, and resistance to cytotoxic stress. Defining the molecular programs that sustain this hierarchy and uncovering vulnerabilities in DNA repair pathways remain central challenges in glioblastoma biology. Here, we used comparative proteomics to map functional differences between GSCs and Differentiated Glioblastoma Cells (DGCs). The analysis revealed a clear dichotomy in cellular states, with GSCs exhibiting a proliferative, biosynthetically active, and DNA repair–associated phenotype, while DGCs showed signatures consistent with metabolic maturation and increased extracellular matrix interaction. We next investigated the impact of RAD52 depletion, a key mediator of homologous recombination and replication stress tolerance. RAD52 inhibition triggered modest but coherent proteomic shifts indicative of increased cellular stress and reduced mesenchymal-associated programs. Despite these changes, core stem-like signatures remained largely stable, suggesting that RAD52 is not essential for maintaining stem-like identity under the conditions tested. Together, these findings define distinct proteomic programs underlying glioblastoma cellular hierarchy and suggest that RAD52 primarily supports stress adaptation and phenotypic plasticity rather than stemness maintenance. These results highlight DNA repair dependencies as potential therapeutic entry points to impair tumour adaptability without directly eroding the stem-like compartment.

title: Rational Design of SIRT2 Inhibitors as Potential Glioblastoma Therapeutics Using Combined 3D-QSAR, Docking, and Machine Learning Methods

affiliations.name: University of Belgrade, Faculty of Pharmacy

bodyParagraphs: Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) is a key regulator of apoptosis, DNA repair, and the cell cycle, making it a promising target for anticancer therapy. In glioblastoma, SIRT2 has been implicated in tumor progression and treatment resistance, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target in this malignancy. Achieving high selectivity remains challenging due to the conserved NAD⁺ binding site among sirtuin family members. Derivatives of 5-((3-amidobenzyl)oxy)nicotinamide are among the most potent and selective SIRT2 inhibitors, providing a foundation for further exploration. In this study, a 3D-QSAR model was constructed using 86 nicotinamide-based SIRT2 inhibitors, complemented by GRIND-derived pharmacophore modelling. The model, developed using partial least squares regression, achieved R² = 0.89 and Q² = 0.69, with no outliers in the applicability domain. Model interpretation highlighted the positive influence of steric features, secondary amide groups, and nitrogen atoms in the pyridine ring on SIRT2 activity. Fine-tuning the propynyl and central phenyl groups produced derivatives with predicted enhanced potency. Molecular docking on SIRT1–3 isoforms enabled the development of two machine learning classification models (Naive Bayes and k-nearest neighbours) to predict SIRT1/2 and SIRT2/3 selectivity profiles. Several selective SIRT2 inhibitors were identified in silico, and these will be synthesised and tested in vitro, supporting the development of novel SIRT2-targeted anticancer therapies.

By integrating 3D-QSAR, selectivity modelling, and ADMET predictions, several promising selective SIRT2 inhibitors were identified. These candidates will be synthesised and tested in vitro to validate their efficacy and selectivity, advancing the development of novel SIRT2-targeted anticancer therapies.

title: Repurposing statins as senolytics in pediatric low-grade glioma leverages mevalonate pathway dependency in oncogene-induced senescence

programme.programmeTitle: Repurposing statins as senolytics in pediatric low-grade glioma leverages mevalonate pathway dependency in oncogene-induced senescence
programme.sessionTitle: Pediatric, Low-grade and Rare CNS Tumors

affiliations.name: Hopp Children’s Cancer Center Heidelberg (KiTZ) and German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Germany
Heidelberg University Hospital, Heidelberg, Germany
Medical Faculty, Heidelberg University, Germany

bodyParagraphs: Pediatric low-grade glioma (pLGG) is driven by genetic alterations of the MAPK pathway, that initiate oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) in the majority of pLGG tumor cells. Current therapy, including chemotherapy and MAPK inhibitors, does not target tumor cells in OIS, which serve as source for relapse after therapy cessation. Hence, eradication of senescent tumor cells has the potential to induce durable responses. Our group has shown that BCL-XL is a targetable vulnerability of senescent pLGG cells, but so far clinical translation has been hampered by the lack of approved BCL-XL inhibitors. To identify novel translationally relevant dependencies, we performed a drug repurposing screen using a library comprising approved and brain-penetrant drugs. n=564 drugs were screened in three patient-derived pLGG cell lines. Using the iTReX platform, drug sensitivity scores were calculated to compare drug response between OIS and proliferation. Top hit drugs were validated using metabolic activity assays and high-content microscopy. Drug interaction with standard of care therapy and BCL-XL inhibitors was assessed. Analysis of gene and protein expression and pathway rescue experiments were used to investigate downstream metabolic dependencies and the mode of cell death induction. The two HMG-CoA-reductase inhibitors (statins) lovastatin and atorvastatin, that block the mevalonate pathway, were identified as top hit drugs with senolytic activity. Intriguingly, in-class senolytic properties were validated with brain-penetrant and pediatric approved statins, fluvastatin and pitavastatin, at clinically achievable concentrations. Synergy assessment revealed enhanced senolysis in combination with BCL-XL inhibitors. Rescue of statin-induced cytotoxicity with mevalonate verified on-target activity. Among downstream mevalonate pathway metabolites, geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) was identified as a survival dependency. In summary, statins were identified as a novel and clinically approved senolytic drug class in pLGG with high translational potential. The mevalonate-GGPP pathway, a critical regulator of autophagy and vesicle trafficking, was discovered as an actionable pathway in senescent pLGG.

title: Rewiring glioblastoma immunity: the role of EGFL7-Integrin β2 axis

bodyParagraphs: Background: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive form of malignant brain cancer, characterized by an immunosuppressive microenvironment and immune evasion. Despite the success of immune checkpoint inhibitors in other cancers, immunotherapies such as anti-PD1 have shown limited efficacy in glioblastoma, underscoring the need to identify tumor-intrinsic mechanisms that sustain this immunosuppressive microenvironment and to develop more effective therapeutic strategies targeting them. Previously, the secreted factor epidermal growth factor-like protein 7 (EGFL7) has been shown to promote brain tumor growth by affecting the glioblastoma microenvironment (GME). However, its impact on the immune system remains enigmatic. Material and Methods: Using in vivo glioma models, the role of EGFL7 in shaping the immune landscape in glioblastoma was studied through single cell RNA-sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, flow cytometry and mass spectrometry, and analysis of human patient data to corroborate our study. Results: Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of immune cells derived from glioblastoma revealed that EGFL7 promotes an immunosuppressive GME, characterized by enhanced T cell exhaustion and polarization of macrophages towards a protumorigenic state. To uncover the underlying mechanism driving this immunomodulation, proteomic profiling of EGFL7’s interactome in glioma revealed its interaction with integrin β2 (ITGB2), an immune cell surface receptor involved in cell adhesion and migration. Building on this finding, genetic perturbation of the EGFL7-ITGB2 interaction attenuated immunosuppression by limiting T cell exhaustion and reducing polarization of macrophages towards a pro-tumorigenic state, along with prolonging the survival of glioblastoma-bearing mice. Remarkably, a combinatorial regimen of anti-EGFL7 and checkpoint inhibitor anti-PD1 improved the efficacy of the drug, which by itself has not improved glioma patient survival so far. Conclusion: Our study provides unequivocal evidence that EGFL7 mediates immune evasion in glioblastoma and has great potential to serve as an add-on drug target to improve the efficacy of immunotherapies which are not functional in glioblastoma patients so far.

title: Role of ZBTB18 in O-GlcNAcylation in glioblastoma

affiliations.name: University of Insubria
University of Freiburg
Medical Center-University of Freiburg

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor. We have identified Zinc finger and BTB domain-containing protein 18 (ZBTB18) as a potential glioma suppressor whose downregulation is related to poor patients’ outcome. Our preliminary metabolomics analysis, further confirmed by western blot, indicates that the re-expression of ZBTB18 in GBM cell lines reduces the amount of O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc), responsible for the O-GlcNAcylation process, a post-translational modification that involves the attachment of O-GlcNAc moieties to serine and threonine of proteins, and that could promote tumorigenesis by coordinating glycolysis and the TCA cycle. Aberrant O-GlcNAcylation might contribute to metabolic disorders, such as insulin resistance, suggesting it could also play a role in the altered metabolism occurring in cancer cells. In the brain, this reversible and dynamic glycosylation is involved in essential processes, such as synaptic activity and neuronal morphogenesis.

Interestingly, GFPT2, a key limiting enzyme involved in the production of O-GlcNAc, belongs to the group of mesenchymal signature genes in GBM and it is regulated by ZBTB18, as confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis. O-GlcNAcylation is controlled by two enzymes, O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA). Therefore, we sought to identify proteins modified upon ZBTB18 re-expression using the PTMScan® O-GlcNAc [GlcNAc-S/T] Motif Kit (Cell Signaling), followed by mass spectrometry. We identified a few candidates showing increased or reduced O-GlcNAcylation upon exposure to TMG, an OGA inhibitor, or ZBTB18 re-expression, respectively. These pieces of evidence suggest that O-GlcNAcylation may play an important part in ZBTB18 tumor repressive function.

title: Single-cell RNA-sequencing in tumour-bearing humanized mice recapitulates human meningioma and refines preclinical drug discovery.

affiliations.name: University of Plymouth

bodyParagraphs: NF2-related schwannomatosis frequently leads to the development of multiple meningiomas responsible for increased morbidity and mortality. Until now, patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models have been generated in immunocompromised mice, which lack a robust immune-cell tumour microenvironment, a critical driver of meningioma tumorigenesis and progression. For the first time, we are using humanized mice engrafted with CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells prior to meningioma PDX, to analyse the tumour immune cell compartment by single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq), to inform how concordant immune cell infiltration is to human meningiomas and also to identify immunotherapeutic targets and generate a refined model for NF2-deficient meningiomas.

Sc-RNAseq revealed accurate delineation of mouse, human meningioma and human immune cells. KT21-MG1, NCH93 and CH157 meningioma PDXs grew with significantly differential growth kinetics and tumour burdens compared to PDXs in non-humanized controls. ScRNA-seq revealed abundances and expression profiles of PDX immune infiltrates: for example, in KT21-MG1 PDXs (n=5), human immune cells accounted for on average 42% of total microenvironment cells with macrophages being the most abundant, followed by dendritic cells, NK cells and T cells. M2-polarized macrophages in the tumour expressed high levels of SPP1, which positively regulates macrophage infiltration and immune checkpoint activity. T cells and macrophages expressed immune checkpoint markers PD1, PD-L1 and CTLA4. We are currently benchmarking brigatinib in humanized and naïve controls and will compare to immunotherapies in vivo. Humanized mice meningioma PDXs were viable with no evidence of graft-versus-host disease. ScRNA-seq revealed immune-cell infiltrates concordant with human NF2-null meningioma. Interestingly, we saw that top-upregulated antigens in a human immune cell atlas were also expressed abundantly in humanized PDXs. Overall, humanized meningioma PDX mice represent a major refinement to existing immunocompromised models, and incorporating them into NF2-null drug discovery pipelines has the potential to yield more powerful and translational drug efficacy data.

bodyParagraphs: Background: Paediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG) represent the most common CNS tumours in children. Despite established histopathological diagnostics, diagnostic uncertainty persists, particularly for rare entities. The added value of systematic DNA methylation profiling in a population-based diagnostic setting has not been comprehensively quantified. Methods: We analysed 1,173 tumours from the prospective, near population-based, Germany-wide HIT-

LOGGIC registry over a five-year period, integrating histopathology with systematic DNA methylation profiling. We assessed the impact of methylation profiling on diagnostic precision, CNS WHO grading, and epidemiological classification. Results: DNA methylation profiling changed the diagnosis in 5.7% of externally diagnosed cases, including 22 patients with a change in CNS WHO grade, and enabled definitive classification in 71.7% of 205 histologically ambiguous tumours. Five high-grade tumours (0.4%) were newly identified that had not been recognised as such by histology alone. Integration of methylation profiling substantially expanded and diversified the diagnostic spectrum, with marked increases in the detection of rare entities such as diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour (DLGNT), pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), and diffuse astrocytoma with MYB/MYBL1 alteration (LGG MYB), refining epidemiological estimates for paediatric low-grade CNS tumours. Conclusion: Systematic implementation of DNA methylation profiling in paediatric neuro-oncology improves diagnostic precision, supports clinical decision-making, and refines epidemiological estimates in pLGG, supporting its adoption as a routine component of diagnostic workflows.

title: The spatial distribution of tryptophan metabolic fields promote niche specific immunosuppressive programs in gliomas

programme.programmeTitle: The spatial distribution of tryptophan metabolic fields promote niche-specific immunosuppressive programs in gliomas

affiliations.name: DKTK Division of Metabolic crosstalk in cancer, German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), Heidelberg, Germany

bodyParagraphs: Tryptophan (Trp) metabolism leads to the production of neurotransmitters, protective and neurotoxic metabolites. Trp catabolizing enzymes (TCEs) produce a plethora of metabolites that drive immune suppression and cell motility. In particular, indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) and tryptophan-2,3-dioxygenase 2 (TDO2) which produce kynurenine (Kyn), and interleukin-4 induced 1 (IL4I1), which generates indole-3-pyruvate (I3P), mediate these immune suppressive effects by activating the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR). Glioma cells strictly select one main TCE for catabolizing Trp, with extreme rare events showing more than one TCE expressed in the same cell. Moreover, TCEs are found to be dominating certain glioma and microenvironment cell types. Analyzing spatial data showed that TCEs, although sparsely expressed, follow a clear spatial distribution leading to niche specific immunosuppressive programs. Our AI models demonstrate that these effects are due to specific metabolite distribution patterns, specifically those of kynurenine (Kyn) and indole-3-pyruvate (I3P). We applied vision transformer AI models to map these spatial metabolic fields and we were able to use HE slide sections to classify patient tumors based on high and low Trp metabolic activity. We show that glioma patient tumors with high Trp metabolic activity fuels an immunosuppressive microenvironment only upon immunotherapy and not upon standard of care. The high Trp active patients had a four times higher hazard and worse outcome. Our AI models provide a proof of concept for streamlined integration of Trp activity in standard clinical routine. Moreover, our models will improve the stratification of glioma patients to immunotherapies.

title: Time limited add-on of vinblastine to targeted therapy with selumetinib for NF1 associated pediatric low-grade glioma – a Phase 2 study proposal

bodyParagraphs: Background: Pediatric Neurofibromatosis type 1-associated low-grade gliomas (NF1-pLGG), particularly optic pathway gliomas, represent a unique subset of pLGG due to their impact on visual outcome besides other tumor associated burden. Vinblastine first-line monotherapy has shown long-term antitumoral benefit in NF1-pLGG and has become a standard of care option. Recently, the oral MEK-inhibitor selumetinib demonstrated radiological tumor reduction as well as visual improvement in relapsed/progressive NF1-pLGG. However, the 5yr-progression-free survival was significantly lower when compared to vinblastine monotherapy. Combining MEK inhibition with vinblastine in first-line therapy may offer an advantage to preserve visual acuity, increase duration response and reduce treatment burden in this chronic disease. Study design: We propose a multicenter Phase 2 trial for NF1-pLGG patients. Inclusion criteria contain the NCI criteria of NF1 diagnosis and indication for antitumoral pLGG-treatment, including visual deterioration. Exclusion criteria are age below 2 years and prior antitumoral or any treatment with a MEK inhibitor. Antitumoral treatment will consist of 6 months of weekly vinblastine intravenously and oral selumetinib for 26 cycles of 28 days. The protocol will be based on the Master Protocol EU-PEARL NF1 Version 1.0. We define following primary endpoints: radiologic response rate (RAPNO-LGG) and visual improvement rate after 6 months (Snellen/TAC2 or other equivalent measures). Secondary endpoints are mainly radiologic response rate and visual improvement rate after 12 months. Other secondary endpoints include progression-free-and overall-survival and duration of response and treatment-free interval and patient-reported outcome measures. Exploratory endpoints such as safety and tolerability and biomarker correlates complete the study design.
