title: Transcriptomic signature and cellular plasticity of glioblastoma circulating tumor cells

affiliations.name: fondazione pisana per la scienza
Ospedale Livorno

bodyParagraphs: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most aggressive and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. The presence of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the peripheral blood has been well-documented. CTC-based liquid biopsy represents a promising, non-invasive tool for longitudinal disease monitoring. Methods Peripheral blood samples were collected from 4 patients diagnosed with GBM. CTCs were enriched using the Parsortix microfluidic platform. To eliminate false positives arising from background leukocyte contamination and microfluidic-induced shear stress, we performed RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) in parallel on both the enriched CTC pool and matched background blood cells (BC) from the same patient, subjected to the exact same Parsortix protocol. Differential gene expression analysis (log2 Fold Change> 1) and functional enrichment analysis (MSigDB Hallmark 2020) were performed by comparing CTCs against their matched BC controls (CTCs vs BC) to isolate a pure CTC signature. Results The patient-matched background subtraction strategy successfully isolated highly specific transcriptomic alterations in GBM CTCs. MSigDB Hallmark pathway analysis revealed a robust and statistically significant enrichment in Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) (p = 3.72x10^-4), KRAS Signaling Down (p = 4.96x10^-3), Myogenesis, and Coagulation pathways in CTCs. Conversely, CTCs demonstrated a significant down-regulation of pathways associated with the inflammatory response and TNF-alpha Signaling via NF-kB (p = 2.50x10^-5). At the single-transcript level, CTCs exhibited an up-regulation of stem/proneural markers such as SOX2, classical GBM markers including GFAP and S100B. In contrast, prominent mesenchymal markers were either down-regulated or unchanged (e.g., CHI3L1, SERPINE1), suggesting a distinct state of fluid-phase cellular plasticity. Conclusions and Future Perspectives These preliminary data highlight the activation of specific survival and plasticity programs (EMT) during hematogenous dissemination. Ongoing work focuses on directly comparing this clean circulating signature with the primary solid tumor transcriptome of the same patients to map clonal evolution, tumor heterogeneity, and mechanisms of therapy resistance.

title: Transcriptomics and proteomics pave the way to the identification of novel regulators of plasticity in Glioblastoma

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor, strongly resistant to therapy and associated with poor survival. Increasing evidence suggests that phenotypic plasticity, defined as the ability of tumor subpopulations to switch between distinct cellular states, contributes to therapy escape. Although the coexistence of multiple GBM states is well established, the mechanisms sustaining their plasticity remain unclear. Here, we investigated intra-tumoral heterogeneity and plasticity in 3D GBM models. Transcriptional profiles of primary GBM samples revealed marked heterogeneity, consistent with the coexistence of distinct cell states. Based on our data and previous observations, we selected CD44 and CD24 cell-surface markers to identify and isolate subpopulations from a GBM sample (CL_L0627). Notably, only the CD24-negative subpopulations were able to reconstitute the parental population, which we therefore defined as plastic. To assess whether this phenotype was present also in vivo, we performed orthotopic xenograft experiments. Tumors derived from CD24-negative cells displayed increased growth compared with those generated from CD24-positive cells, suggesting that the plastic subpopulation is a major driver of tumor expansion. To uncover the mechanisms underlying plasticity in vitro, we integrated bulk-RNAseq and proteomics analyses. Plastic cells showed selective enrichment of mitochondria-related pathways and increased mitochondrial ROS levels, without changes in mitochondrial mass, indicating that metabolic rewiring may support proliferation and cell-state transitions. Conversely, non-plastic cells were enriched for glycogen metabolism and extracellular vesicle-related pathways, suggesting a possible metabolic and paracrine supportive role. Finally, transcriptomic analyses determined an enrichment of Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) genes, with intriguingly distinct signatures in plastic and non-plastic cells. These results suggest that Polycomb may act as an upstream regulator of alternative cellular states, orchestrating differential epigenetic landscapes consistent with its role in cellular identity. Future studies will determine whether PRC2-dependent chromatin regulation and mitochondrial rewiring cooperate to sustain GBM plasticity and aggressiveness.

bodyParagraphs: Background: Low-grade gliomas (LGG) represent the most common pediatric solid tumors. The HIT-LOGGIC registry accrues over 350 newly diagnosed pediatric LGG cases annually. Tumor-related epilepsy (TRE) is a common clinical symptom. In a subset of patients, seizures may be the first and occasionally, the only manifestation of the disease. Several factors have been proposed to influence the risk of TRE, including tumor location and specific neuropathological subtypes. This study aims to investigate potential clinical and histopathological risk factors associated with seizure occurrence. Methods: Clinical data are collected using standardized questionnaires and clinical reports. Integrated neuropathological diagnostics are performed at reference centers using epigenetic methylation analysis as well as DNA and RNA panel sequencing. Imaging evaluations are conducted at the registry’s national reference center. The influence of potential clinical, radiological, and molecular factors on refractory epilepsy and on clinical outcome is analyzed. Results: We identified a cohort of 246 patients with pediatric LGG and TRE. The age at diagnosis ranged from 2 weeks to 19 years. In 85.3% of cases, epileptic seizures were the first clinical symptom. Glioneuronal tumors such as gangliogliomas and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors were the most common neuropathological entities, accounting for 65 (30.1%) and 47 (21.8%) cases, respectively. A BRAF V600E mutation was detected in 42% patients. 86.2% of tumors are located in the cerebral hemisphere, most frequently in the temporal lobe. 98 patients had treatment-resistant epilepsy. In 108 cases, surgical interventions were performed with the primary goal of achieving seizure freedom. In 76.9% of these cases, a Class 1 seizure outcome was achieved according to the classification of the International League Against Epilepsy.

Conclusion: Identifying potential risk factors for seizures is essential for early recognition and appropriate management. This work highlights the importance of interdisciplinary care in the treatment of pLGG, particularly in patients affected by TRE.

title: WNT6 modulates extracellular vesicle biogenesis and cargo loading in glioblastoma: implications for liquid biopsies

bodyParagraphs: Introduction: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor, characterized by poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Our team showed that WNT6, a Wnt signaling ligand, is overexpressed in GBM and associated with tumor aggressiveness. Notably, WNT6 was highly enriched in extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from GBM primary cells. Given the role of EVs in intercellular communication and their potential as minimally invasive liquid biopsy tools, this work explores the biological and clinical relevance of WNT6-driven EV signaling in GBM. Methods: GBM cell lines with genetically altered WNT6 expression were used. Additionally, plasma from GBM (n=20) and lower grade glioma (n=14) patients were collected from Hospital de Braga. EVs were isolated from conditioned medium (size exclusion chromatography) and plasma (precipitation) and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis and western blot. Transcriptomic (RNA-seq) and proteomic (MS/MS) profiles of cells and EVs were assessed by differential expression and pathway analyses, including GO enrichment and GSEA. WNT6 levels in EVs were quantified by western blot, ddPCR and ELISA. Results: RNA-seq and MS/MS analyses of WNT6-high cells revealed enriched EV and exosome-related signatures. Consistently, WNT6-high cells released more EVs per cell compared to WNT6-low. This effect was reflected in patient samples, where plasma EV concentration was increased in WNT6-high tumors, highlighting a link between WNT6 and EV biogenesis. Furthermore, WNT6 reshaped EV transcriptomic and proteomics cargo, with enrichment in oncogenic pathways. Interestingly, WNT6 mRNA and protein were detected in EVs from GBM cells and patient plasma, closely mirroring its cellular and tumoral expression levels, respectively. Conclusion: WNT6 modulates EV release and shapes oncogenic EV cargo in GBM. Additionally, its detectability in circulating EVs, reflecting tumor expression levels, supports its potential as a liquid biopsy biomarker in glioma.

title: Modeling SHH medulloblastoma and treatment-induced neurodevelopmental alterations using Human cerebellar organoids

affiliations.name: Inserm U1245 Cancer and Brain Genomics
Rouen University
Kavli Institute of Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK

bodyParagraphs: Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)–type medulloblastomas are embryonal tumors that disrupt cerebellar cortex development. Although survival rates reach 75–88%, many survivors experience long-term cognitive and emotional impairments. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy treatments contribute to these sequelae, highlighting the need to understand their underlying mechanisms on both healthy and tumoral tissues. Loss of function of PTCH1, a key SHH pathway receptor, promotes abnormal proliferation of cerebellar progenitors and tumorigenesis.

We generated cerebellar organoids from wild-type human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and hiPSCs carrying heterozygous PTCH1 inactivation (PTCH1+/−). The effects of SHH-targeted therapies were assessed using Vismodegib or JQ1, administered either acutely (day 28) or chronically (28, 35 and 42). Cerebellar and SHH pathway gene expression was analyzed by RTqPCR. Major cell markers, as well as primary cilia bearing the Ptch1 receptor, were analyzed by immunohistochemistry. Spontaneous electrical activity was recorded in mature organoids using microelectrode arrays, and the involvement of GABAergic and glutamatergic receptors was investigated.

In healthy organoids, Vismodegib inhibited SHH signaling, as shown by complete loss of GLI1 expression, and unexpectedly induced a ciliopathy characterized by predominantly biciliated cells. JQ1 exacerbated this phenotype, leading to multiciliated cells. Organoids developed functional neuronal networks involving GABA-A receptors, while Vismodegib reduced spontaneous activity. PTCH1+/− organoids displayed increased growth but preserved structural and electrophysiological features. Following Vismodegib treatment, they similarly showed complete GLI1 loss and multiciliation.

Recently, we established a new invasion model by introducing SHH-group medulloblastoma cells into healthy cerebellar organoids, providing a physiologically relevant system to investigate tumor–cerebellar interactions. We aim to use this model to further assess how anticancer therapies affect both medulloblastoma invasion and the surrounding healthy cerebellar tissue.

Overall, cerebellar organoids reveal how SHH-targeted therapies disrupt ciliogenesis and neuronal activity, providing a human-relevant platform to decipher treatment-induced neurodevelopmental defects and refine therapeutic strategies in SHH medulloblastoma.

title: Comparative genetic analyses of glioblastoma-stem-cell based brain tumor organoids vs glioblastoma stem like cells and glioblastoma tissue

affiliations.name: Saxonian Incubator for Clinical Translation (SIKT), University of Leipzig
Department of Neurosurgery, University Hospital Leipzig

bodyParagraphs: Glioblastoma (GB) is defined as high grade glioma with an astrocytic differentiation (WHO grade 4). Possibly, glioblastoma stem like cells (GSC) could be responsible for tumor initiation, maintenance, recurrence and cancer therapy resistance. Genetic comparisons of glioblastoma tissue vs GSCs and GSC-based brain tumor organoids (GSC-BTO) are still limited. The aim of this study was the genetic comparison of tumor tissue, GSC and GSC-BTO to assess the genetic integrity of GSC-BTO.

Primary tumor was obtained during neurosurgical resection and GSCs were cultivated under serum-free conditions. GSC-based organoids were generated using StemDiff™ Cerebral Organoid Kit. Immunhistochemical characterization of GSCs (e.g. SOX2, Nestin) and GSC-BTO (e.g. GFAP, ß-Tubulin) was performed. Genetic analyses were carried out using SNP array (Affymetrix CytoScanHD Array). In previously published data (PMID: 32634135), we have detected a similar genetic profile of tumor tissue vs GSC with minor differences. Here, we could identified previously detected chromosomal aberrations in tumor tissue and GSC for GSC-BTO too (e.g. gain 3q21.3-q29). Predominantly, we identified a comparable genetic profile for GSC-BTO in comparison with GSC or tumor tissue of the respective patient with few additional aberrations in GSC-BTO. One donor have showed more chromosomal aberrations in GSC-BTO vs GSC and tumor tissue (e.g. loss of 1q21.2-q44 and gain 8q11.1-q24.3 in GSC-BTO). Interestingly, in this donor, the cn-LOH aberration for chromosomal region 9p21.3-p21.1 were detected only in GSC-BTO (tumor: -; GSC: loss) and could be an indication for a tumor repair mechanisms (somatic reduplication).

Predominantly, our results highlights the reflection of the respective patient specific genetic profile of GSC-BTO vs tumor tissue and GSC. Nevertheless, further investigations are needed to enlarge the knowledge about the genetic integrity of glioblastoma-based tumor organoids.
